title: Road-type field codes motorways and dual carriageways separately only in 2013-2015, so the conventional and motorway figures describe the coding, not the roads
disclosure_where: Nothing on catalonia.html, Figure 1 or data.html Table 18. DATA_QUALITY_MICRODATA.md:373 gives pooled counts only. The only related remarks concern the cross-source harmonised model: data.html ('11 of 12 candidate variables ... (road type does not)'), validation.html ('Road type was left out because its coding disagrees on the crashes both sources hold'), methodology.md ('road class fails'), GENERALISABILITY.md:413, and ml_common_feature_validation.csv (road_class JSD 0.056). None says the Catalan field is coded differently by year, none qualifies the Catalonia page's road-type figures, and the validation page puts road-type coding breaks down to DGT's records.
factual_core: The Servei Català de Trànsit file's road-type field (D_TIPUS_VIA) codes motorways (Autopista) and dual carriageways (Autovia) almost only in 2013-2015. In 2010-2012 and 2016-2023, crashes on those roads are coded 'Carretera convencional'. The pooled 2010-2023 road-type figures on the Catalonia page therefore mix coding regimes and misdescribe roads: 1,981 of 3,093 fatal crashes on conventional roads, 18.8% of 10,540, and motorways at 20.5% from 'only 224 crashes' with an interval that overlaps conventional roads.
materiality: Fatal crashes on conventional roads would be about 1,460-1,620 of 3,093 (47-52%), or at most 1,801 (58%) under the strictest rule, instead of 1,981 (64%). 'Most' is therefore not established. The conventional fatal share would be about 17.6-17.9% (18.9% under the hard rule) instead of 18.8%, on about 8,300-8,600 crashes, not 10,540. Motorway crashes would number about 700-1,250 (3 to 5.6 times 224). Their fatal share would be 22.4-25.0%, with lower 95% bounds of 20.2-22.3%, above every reclassified conventional upper bound (18.4-19.7%), so the overlap clause reverses. DGT's own coding of the 2016-2023 crashes gives 24.4% against 17.3%. Dual carriageways would go from 496 crashes at 16.5% to about 1,700 at 19.5-21.5%, above conventional roads, which changes the ordering in Figure 1 and Table 18. 'Motorways had the highest share' survives. Spillover, not quantified: the calculator's State and regional (reference) conventional levels contain about 36% and 30% motorway and dual-carriageway crashes, and the model has no year term.
suggested_fix: Restrict the road-type shares to 2013-2015, the years the file codes motorways and autovias. Alternatively, reclassify from the road name (and km point): DGT's TIPO_VIA for 2016-2023 and a road or section template for 2010-2012. At minimum: state next to the paragraph, Figure 1 and Table 18 that the file codes motorways and dual carriageways separately only in 2013-2015; delete 'only 224 crashes' and the overlap clause; replace '1,981 of the 3,093' and 'most' with 'about half'; add a year-by-year road-type check to regional.py. Review the calculator's road levels for the same break.

title: Location contrasts (lead's 6.63, Table 1, 'urban crossing 8.75') are inflated by an outcome-dependent 'alignment unknown' level
disclosure_where: data.html, 'Missing values and regional recording' (repeated in docs/methodology.md §13 and docs/models/dgt_crash_severity.md). It says the level is 95.7% Catalan and 'describes recording practice'. It says 'A recording practice that goes with the outcome could distort the other coefficients through such a level' and refits without Catalonia, with 'All 32 other odds ratios stay inside the full model's interval' and the urban-crossing zone term moving from 4.28 to 2.57. Table 17 there shows the interurban zone moving 3.24→2.00 and the conventional road type 2.04→2.68. The model card says the level 'marks crashes recorded in Cataluña rather than a kind of road'. No document says that Catalan alignment is filled in almost only for severe crashes. The joint contrasts are never refitted. severity.html (the lead, Table 1 and the 8.75 sentence) has no caveat beyond a CSV link.
factual_core: In DGT's Catalan records, road alignment (TRAZADO_PLANTA) on non-street crashes is filled in almost only when someone died or was hospitalised within 24 h. Inside Catalonia, the model's 'alignment unknown' level (OR 0.12) therefore stands in for the outcome. The Catalan crashes whose alignment is recorded are selected for severity, and they feed the zone and road terms, so the joint location contrasts in the lead and Table 1 come out too high, the urban-crossing rows most of all.
materiality: Conventional interurban: 6.63 becomes 4.97–6.23 across seven leakage-free specifications. The published value is 6–33% too high, but every alternative lies inside its interval and the direction holds. The four interurban road types go from 5.66–7.23 to roughly 4.4–5.8 (at most 6.2). Urban-crossing conventional goes from 8.75 to 3.76–6.87, so it is 27–133% too high; five of the seven estimates fall below the published lower bound of 6.52, and it is the largest contrast in only 2 of 7. Urban crossing/urban street goes from 4.28 to 1.82–2.73, urban crossing/other road from 7.47 to 3.30–4.86, and interurban motorway from 7.23 to 4.41–5.87.
suggested_fix: Refit the lead and Table 1 location contrasts with Catalan alignment neutralised, either set to the reference or with alignment dropped (for example with province fixed effects), and publish that version or the range. State on severity.html that Catalan alignment is recorded almost only for crashes with a death or a hospitalisation within 24 h. Remove the implied 'largest' ranking of the urban crossing and the site check 'a conventional road through a town has the largest location contrast'.

title: 'Did not last' exists only because the pre-trend is limited to bends; by the page's own QAIC rule, a 2004 level shift fits the pre-period better and two bends fit equally, and both give a lasting ~10% fall
disclosure_where: site/policy.html, right after the heading: 'The result depends on how the earlier trend is projected. A straight line gives ... a lasting fall, -9.5% on average ... That difference favours the bend without being decisive.' site/data.html adds 'it is still a selection step, which is why the alternative pre-trends ... are reported', and docs/methodology.md §14 says 'a preference, not decisive evidence'. Nowhere (pages, methodology, STATISTICAL_AUDIT, CLAIM_LEDGER) mentions level-shift or multi-change pre-trends, or other window starts. The Table 5 sentence 'every specification except the straight-line pre-trend' rests on 10 of 12 rows that share the Aug 2003 knot.
factual_core: Under the page's own pre-trend rule (QAIC on Jan 2000-Jun 2006 only, c = 1.6076, two parameters per searched change), an equally parsimonious level-shift pre-trend (Jan 2004) fits the pre-period better than the chosen Aug 2003 bend (QAIC 473.4 vs 476.2), and a two-bend trend ties (476.26). Both give a lasting 17-month fall (-11.5%, -9.5%) instead of the published transient -2.5%. So 'did not last' depends on allowing only continuous single bends.
materiality: Only single continuous bends (and the quadratic) support these statements: the heading 'An immediate fall of about 7% that did not last', 'rejoin the projected path in about July 2007', 'the earlier months favour a trend that bends once', and the summary's single figure -2.5% (-7.8% to +3.2%). Under pre-trends that the pre-period fits as well or slightly better: - The step is -9.5% to -12.6%. - The 17-month change ranges from about -1% to -12.5% across specifications and window starts. - QAIC-weighted averages give about -7% to -8% for the 17-month change (intervals about -15% to 0%) and about -10% for the step. The summary's 'cannot show ... that it lasted' and the non-attribution conclusion survive, because the model-averaged intervals reach zero. The heading's 'did not last' and the -2.5% as the estimate do not survive. This is an overstatement, not a disclosed limitation: the disclosure tells readers the pre-period favours the transient pattern, but under an equally parsimonious extension it slightly favours a lasting fall.
suggested_fix: Change the heading to say the persistence of the fall cannot be determined. In the summary, replace the single -2.5% with the range across pre-trends: bend, early-2004 level shift, shift plus slope change, two bends, and window starts. Alternatively, give a QAIC-weighted average with unconditional intervals: 17-month change about -7% to -8%, interval reaching zero; step about -10%. Say that the pre-2006 change can be fitted as a bend in 2003 or as a drop in early 2004, and that the two disagree on whether the fall lasted. Qualify 'the earlier months favour a trend that bends once' and 'the decline had already steepened in 2003'.

title: The 2.68 figure is printed with only its sampling interval; the 1.49–3.63 sensitivity range was removed from the home and drivers pages

factual_core: The home page (Main findings), the drivers page (lead and per-km paragraph), Figure 1 and the driver-risk tool give the 18-29 per-km ratio 2.68 with only its 95% sampling interval of 2.5-2.9. materiality: The number 2.68 and the direction (more often under every alternative, minimum 1.49) do not change. The uncertainty shown with the headline is about ±7% (2.48-2.86), while the authors' own range is 1.49-3.63 (-44%/+36%), 5-6 times wider. The same applies on the drivers page and in the tool to 30-44 (1.18-1.31 against a range of 1.12-1.72) and 65-74 (1.0-1.2 against 0.67-1.70). The fix is one clause in each sentence.
suggested_fix: Restore the range beside 2.68 on index.html, drivers.html, Figure 1 and the tool, e.g. '(95% sampling interval 2.5-2.9; 1.5 to 3.6 times under the other assumptions tested)', or lead with 'more often under every assumption tested, about 1.5 to 3.6 times'. Do the same for 30-44 and 65-74. Relax tests/test_site.py:501/1006 accordingly. Otherwise correct data.py:1337 and the drivers.py docstring.

How much they depend on the surveys is on the drivers page'. The condition, range and conclusion are on the linked drivers and methodology pages only. It states the Madrid-split conditional estimate (2.43) as a plain fact with only its 95% sampling interval (2.0-3.0, wholly above 1). On its default view the tool presents as an established excess (2.0-3.0 times as often) what the drivers page says the data do not establish. The sentence needs the Madrid condition and the 0.97-3.20 range (and 0.67-1.70 at 65-74, which the tool also shows bare), or a different default comparison. The 0.91 against 18-29 also needs its 0.73-1.15 interval.

Give the cross-group ratio its interval. Extend test_the_conditional_75_plus_estimate_is_never_read_alone to the tool's rendered text.

title: 'One series' / 'same basis' contradicts DGT's own 2024 report, which declares a different methodology
disclosure_where: None. Searching site/*.html and docs/methodology.md finds no mention of the 2024 method change, IDIADA or the new filter. tests/test_site.py:878 forbids 'different method' on trends.html and vehicles.html.
factual_core: Five published passages describe DGT's 2022-2024 kilometre figures as comparable. data.html says 'gives the mean distance driven per vehicle for 2022, 2023 and 2024 as one series' and, in the vehicle notes, 'on the same basis'. sources.html says 'as one series'. methodology.md:225 says 'so 2022-2024 are estimates on one basis'. methodology.md:697-699 says 'on the same basis', directly after describing the 2022 km as 'annualised over inspection readings taken across 2014-2023'. DGT's own 2024 report contradicts all of this. It says the 2024 estimates use a methodology different from the 2023 publication: 2024 inspections only (earlier exercises used several years), a new 99.5th-percentile filter and new variables. It says these changes produced differences in some values. Its Table 6 presents the three years as 'tres ejercicios de estimación', each row copied from its own exercise.
materiality: Every 2022-2024 change the site takes from DGT's kilometres crosses the change of estimator DGT itself declares: - car mean -6.0%; - vehicle-km -1.6%; - km per tonne -3.0%; - deaths per km +3.9%. On the step DGT calls the same approach (2022 to 2023), vehicle-km rose +0.8% and km per tonne +1.9%. The headline analyses do not rest on these figures: - Since 2019 and the long run use fuel; - the vehicles page uses 2022 only; - the drivers page uses ratios. The damage is confined to the technical notes and the side check (I2, I3).
suggested_fix: Say that DGT's 2024 release tabulates three separate estimation exercises: 2022 and 2023 by ONSV, and 2024 by IDIADA with a method DGT says changed some values. Changes from 2022 to 2024 therefore mix real change with a change of estimator; give 2022-2023 as the only broadly like-for-like step. Correct methodology.md:220-226 and 697-699, the data.html and sources.html wording, tests/test_site.py:878 and CLAIM_LEDGER row ledger-B|66.

title: 'Points the other way' rests on the method break; on consistent bases DGT's km per tonne rises
disclosure_where: The sentence in the data.html long-run notes adds only 'which start in 2022' and 'On all roads, deaths per kilometre are not measured'. The section it links to calls the DGT figures 'one series'.
factual_core: The published line is 'The other source of kilometres points the other way: ... kilometres per tonne of fuel 3.0% lower in 2024 than in 2022'. The whole -3.0% comes from the 2023 to 2024 step (-4.8%), which crosses DGT's declared method change. On the same-approach step, 2022 to 2023, DGT km per tonne rose +1.9%. That is the same direction as: - the Ministry's interurban measure (+3.4%, 2022 to 2023); - toll motorways (+5.1%, then +2.85% in 2023 to 2024). The sentence also sets DGT's 2022-2024 change against a Ministry trend over 2019-2023. The code at long_run.py:840-843 prints 'points the other way' whatever the sign.
materiality: The sentence is the site's only counterweight to the Ministry's faster-rising km per tonne. The site itself says that rise would put the 2023 per-fuel excess inside its range. Where DGT's estimates share an approach, they rise like the Ministry's. 'Points the other way' therefore has no valid support, and on the overlapping years the evidence points the opposite way. For 2022 to 2024 the direction is not identified. Under different assumptions it runs from the published -3.0% to about +2.6%. The stated conclusions survive: 'depends on ... the kilometres a tonne of fuel represents' and 'not measured'. The weight of evidence shifts toward the per-fuel excess being partly a km-per-tonne artefact. No headline reverses.
suggested_fix: Say that DGT changed method in 2024. On its like-for-like step, 2022 to 2023, km per tonne rose 1.9%, the same direction as the Ministry's. Across the 2024 change the figures fall 3.0%, which cannot be separated from the change of estimator. Add a check on the sign before wording that asserts a direction.

title: The −1.6% vehicle-km and +3.9% deaths per km straddle the method break; their signs are not identified
disclosure_where: data.html says only 'The series starts in 2022, so it cannot be set against 2019 or the long run'. The same paragraph calls the figures 'one series'.
factual_core: data.html reports these as changes along one series: - vehicle-km fell 1.6% (2022 to 2024); - deaths per km rose 3.9%, against 0.8% per tonne of fuel; - the car mean fell from 13,073 to 12,295 km. On DGT's same-approach step, 2022 to 2023, vehicle-km rose +0.80% and deaths per km rose +2.61%, less than per fuel (+4.52%). That is the reverse of the ordering the site reports. The fall in the car mean is concentrated in the 0-4 band (-19.1%). Cars in that band have mostly not yet had their first ITV, so their values are model-imputed. Every older band rose.
materiality: The sign of the 2022-2024 changes is not identified. Deaths per km range from about -1.8% (every 0-4 band at its 2023 mean) through +3.0% (2022 on DGT's substituted basis, I5) to the published +3.9%. The paragraph implies that fuel understates the rise in risk per km. On the same-approach step the ordering reverses. The figures sit in the technical notes, and fuel remains the denominator of the headline, so no headline changes.
suggested_fix: Report 2022 to 2023 as DGT's like-for-like step: vehicle-km +0.8%, deaths per km +2.6% against +4.5% per tonne. Label 2023 to 2024 as crossing a method change. Either drop the 2022-2024 per-km figures or give them as a range under the young-vehicle sensitivity.

title: The 'comparable 2014–2023, +49%' for interurban illegal manoeuvres depends on a threshold 2% above the series' own 2017 jump
disclosure_where: factors.html, next to the claim: 'rose on interurban roads from 25.4% to 37.8%, a level they had already reached by 2017', which signals the step. Under Table 1: the rule 'cannot say whether a break, or a trend within a run, comes from behaviour, from recording or from both'. Technical notes (data.html): 'The threshold is a convention, and every change is published with its test so that another threshold can be applied ... the rule rules out only single-year jumps'. The 1.2234 ratio is in the factor_changes.csv download. Nowhere does the study say that this run sits about 2% under the threshold or would split at 20%. Table 1 still labels it 'Comparable years 2014-2023'. SECOND_AUDIT.md:29 shows the point was raised before and left as the 'by 2017' phrase.
factual_core: From 2016 to 2017 the interurban illegal-manoeuvres share rose x1.2234 (31.9% to 39.0%). Table 1 shows one comparable run, 2014-2023 (+49%), only because BREAK_RATIO = 1.25 is above that ratio. At any threshold of 1.2234 or less (for example 1.20) the series breaks in 2017: 2014-2016 is +26% and 2017-2023 is -3%.
materiality: Under a 20% rule, Table 1's row 'Illegal manoeuvres, Interurban, 2014-2023, 25.4% to 37.8%, +49%' becomes two rows: 2014-2016 +26% and 2017-2023 -3%, and the level is flat after 2017. The share-scale log-linear trend over 2014-2023 is +33% (95% +4% to +69%) and fits a step poorly. The facts in the text (25.4%, 37.8%, the level reached by 2017) stay true. What fails is the 'comparable' label and reading +49% as a change over the decade. No other Table 1 row, and nothing in the lead, changes at 1.20. The summary never mentions manoeuvres, so 'headline' slightly overstates the row's prominence.
suggested_fix: Beside Table 1, or in the manoeuvres sentence, add: 'the 2017 rise of 22% is just under the 25% break rule; at a 20% rule the series breaks in 2017 and is flat from 2017 to 2023 (-3%)'. Alternatively, show the run as 2014-2016 and 2017-2023.

title: Table 1's 'Street / Other road' row includes 14,349 Catalan 2024 urban streets coded 'Otro'
disclosure_where: data.html technical notes ('Zone, road type and illustrative crash profiles'): 'The road type "other" mixes two kinds of crash: in 2024 DGT's records for the four Catalan provinces code urban streets as another kind of road (coding breaks), so its odds ratio, 1.74, rises to 2.40 without Catalonia's crashes.' The 1.74 there is the same number as the Street/Other road row, because street is the zone reference. The coding-breaks section gives 15,531 of the 17,519 code-14 crashes in 2024 as Catalan. data.html also gives the urban-crossing zone odds ratio as 4.28 to 2.57 without Catalonia. severity.html Table 1 and its caption carry no note; the page only links 'technical notes' and the with/without-Catalonia CSV.
factual_core: In 2024 DGT's records for the four Catalan provinces code every street-zone (ZONA 3) crash as TIPO_VIA 14 'Other' instead of 9 'Street'. These crashes fall in the model's 'other road' level, so 14,349 of the 29,209 crashes in Table 1's 'Street / Other road' row are recoded urban streets. Reading them as urban streets materially moves that row and the 'Urban crossing / Urban street' row, which equals the urban-crossing zone coefficient.
materiality: Street/Other road: 1.74 (1.23-2.47) becomes 2.67 (2.09-3.42), +53% and outside the published interval. Urban crossing/Urban street: 4.28 (2.41-7.62) becomes 2.85 (2.16-3.76), -33% and inside the interval. Neither row is quoted in the page prose. The headline numbers are essentially unchanged: conventional interurban 6.63 to 6.68, the 'four interurban road types' range 5.66-7.23 to 5.73-7.28, and urban crossing on a conventional road 8.75 to 8.88.
suggested_fix: In features.PREDICTORS / model_frame, read TIPO_VIA 14 in ZONA 3 for provinces 8, 17, 25 and 43 in 2024 as 'urban street', as the inverted junction flag is already corrected. Alternatively, footnote the two Table 1 rows: about half of the Street/Other road crashes are Catalan urban streets coded 'other' in 2024; read as urban streets, the row is 2.67 (2.09-3.42) and Urban crossing/Urban street 2.85 (2.16-3.76).

title: Catalan weather and surface recording depends on severity; the within-Catalonia wet odds ratio (0.20) is an artefact that pulls the national 0.56 down a little
disclosure_where: data.html Table 17 and its text give the full-model wet odds ratio as 0.62 to 0.72 without Catalonia, 'still below 1'. This is framed as robustness to the alignment-unknown regime, not as a surface-coding artefact. validation.html says Catalan crashes with a death or serious injury differ from Spain's beyond the preset limit on weather and road surface, 'in how crashes are recorded'. severity.html links the 'every odds ratio with and without Catalonia' CSV. No page says that Catalan surface and weather coding depends on severity, and the headline 0.56 is never given its without-Catalonia counterpart, 0.61. The project's own ledger-C|5 computed 0.61 and judged it robust.
factual_core: In DGT's records for the Catalan provinces, crashes with a death or serious injury within 24 h rarely carry a wet surface, and most of those in rain are coded with a dry surface. The province's slight crashes and the rest of Spain do not show this. This outcome-dependent coding gives an extreme wet-surface odds ratio within Catalonia and pulls the national 'about 0.56' slightly down, to about 0.61 without Catalonia.
materiality: The headline wet figure moves from 0.56 (0.49-0.64) to about 0.60-0.61 (0.53-0.68). That is +7-9% on the odds-ratio scale and about 11-15% weaker on the log scale, still within the published interval. Rain is unchanged at 0.57, so 'a wet surface and rain each go with about 0.56' becomes about 0.57-0.61. The full-model wet value in data.html Tables 16 and 17 moves from 0.62 to 0.71-0.72, and the urban-streets-only value from 0.57 to 0.69. Every qualitative claim holds: lower odds, below 1 in every variant, and holding on interurban roads and urban streets separately.
suggested_fix: On severity.html, after 'about 0.56', add: 'DGT's records for the four Catalan provinces seldom record a wet surface in crashes with a death or serious injury, and pair most rain in them with a dry surface, as the Servei Catala de Transit's file does. Without Catalonia's crashes the wet-surface odds ratio is 0.61 (0.54-0.68), and rain's 0.57.' Alternatively, give Catalan surface and weather their own level, as a recording regime, and quote 0.60 (0.53-0.67).

title: On urban streets the heavy-vehicle excess is confined to crashes with pedestrians and two-wheelers; the model's additive flags spread it to car-versus-lorry crashes
disclosure_where: Not disclosed. SEVERITY_CALCULATOR.md:378-380 mentions the model's 'additive structure' only for rare combinations with fewer than 20 similar crashes, and the urban car+heavy side collision has 36. The same report (line 347) states 'on the urban reference crash x2.55 (2.08–3.12)' without a caveat, and sev_contrasts.csv:86 gives the same figure. The calculator shows 9.4% (7.2–12.0%) with no warning.
factual_core: On urban streets, the heavy-vehicle association depends strongly on whether a vulnerable road user (pedestrian, cyclist, moped or motorcycle) is involved, so the published model's additive user flags are rejected there. As a result, the model's urban car-versus-lorry contrast (x2.55; 9.4% vs 3.7%) is not supported by urban crashes between motor vehicles. Adding the term barely moves the interurban headline but cuts the urban reference contrast to about 1.7.
materiality: Headline unaffected: the interurban reference stays at 1.97 (1.89 with both zone terms), so 'about twice' on index.html holds. The published calculator and the linked report overstate the urban car-versus-lorry association: - x2.55 (2.08–3.12) becomes x1.68 (1.33–2.19); - the estimate of 9.4% becomes about 6.3%, which lies outside the calculator's printed interval. Urban crashes involving a vulnerable user and a heavy vehicle are slightly underestimated (pedestrian 18.3% vs 20.5%). A statistician would call this a failed additivity assumption that biases some of a published tool's outputs, not an error in the headline.
suggested_fix: Add a heavy x vulnerable-user term (at least on urban streets) to the calculator model; it improves the nested log loss. Alternatively, state on the model page and in SEVERITY_CALCULATOR.md:347 that on urban streets the excess with lorries and buses comes from crashes with pedestrians, cyclists and motorcyclists, and withdraw the urban x2.55 for crashes between cars and lorries.

title: The owner restriction drops Catalan deaths on Generalitat and State roads whose kilometres are in the denominator; the Catalan owner codes are corrupted and depend on the outcome
disclosure_where: Not disclosed for DGT's records or the road-class rates. - sources.html lists other Catalan coding breaks (the dual-carriageway code, the inverted junction flag) but not the owner field. - data.html and validation.html describe an owner-field artefact only in the separate Servei Català de Trànsit file. - docs/data_inventory.md:223 notes the Catalan jump to owner code 5 but treats it as outside the coverage. - road_class_risk.csv and methodology §5.1 publish the all-owner rate (2023 ratio 3.38), which bounds the effect on the ratio but does not give its cause.
factual_core: In DGT's records for the four Catalan provinces, owner codes 4 and 5 (municipal and other) are put on most interurban crashes on Generalitat C- roads and other numbered regional or provincial roads, and on some State roads. Which code a crash gets depends on whether it was fatal. class_risk keeps only owners 1-3, so it drops deaths and crashes on networks whose vehicle-km are in the table 1.2.14 denominator. The documented swap of codes 4 and 5 happens only in Catalonia.
materiality: 2023 figures: - Conventional rate 7.41 -> 7.55 (+1.8%). - Motorway rate 2.15 -> 2.22 (+3.4%). - Ratio 3.45 -> 3.40 (interval 3.03-3.92 -> 2.99-3.86). - 2016-2023 range 3.04-3.84 -> 3.02-3.77 (2.98-3.76). The heading's '3 to 4 times' is unchanged. Secondary published figures move more: - data.html split 2.28x crashes per km and 1.51x deaths per crash -> 2.40x and 1.42x (+5% and -6%). - The '8.7% to 11.2%' of interurban deaths on municipal and other roads (long-run.html and data.html) -> about 6.6-9.1%, an overstatement of roughly 2 points (about 20-25% relative). The 'less than 1%' conclusion still holds. - The rationale in the docstring, test and methodology ('about one injury crash in five ... roads of municipal and other owners carry many crashes that rarely kill'; the 'codes 4 and 5 swap') is mostly a Catalan coding artefact. - The *_outside_km_coverage CSV columns are mislabelled for Catalonia.
suggested_fix: For the four Catalan provinces, set coverage from the road name: - C-, N-/A-/AP- and the B/BV/BP/GI/GIV/GIP/L/LV/LP/T/TV/TP roads count as covered. - The B-10/B-20 municipal stretches and 'No inventariada' stay outside. title: Newey–West(12) intervals undercover even when the model is right; with valid errors the step and the slope change are not significant
disclosure_where: policy.html lead ('The model's intervals are too narrow: at 6 of the 14 other Julys...'), Figure 2 caption, and the placebo paragraph (calibrated -21% to +3%). data.html model paragraph ('Even so, the July placebos show these model-based intervals to be too narrow'), placebo paragraph ('The other intervals ... probably too narrow as well') and Table 5 caption. Not disclosed anywhere: that the estimator is biased under a correct model, that the residuals are serially uncorrelated (data.html gives month-to-month correlation as the reason for using Newey-West), and what the intervals would be with valid errors.
factual_core: Every interval in the case study uses Newey-West errors with 12 lags and no small-sample correction (policy.py:197, 301). For the main fit (95 months, 16 parameters), the residuals show no serial correlation. The NW12 standard errors are smaller than both the HC0 and the quasi-Poisson ones, and the NW12 intervals undercover badly even when the model is right. With valid model-based errors, neither the step nor the slope change excludes zero.
materiality: Step: -13%..-1% becomes -14%..+1% (quasi-Poisson) or -14%..0% (NB2-ML), so it no longer excludes zero. Slope change: +1.4%..+14.0%/yr becomes -1.7%..+17.6%/yr, so it no longer excludes zero, which removes the statistical support for the 'did not last' reading. 17-month average: -7.8%..+3.2% becomes -9.1%..+4.6%, with the conclusion unchanged. All 12 rows of Table 5, the 'Negative binomial' row included, widen by roughly 10-50%. The page's conclusions ('cannot show that the licence caused the fall, or that it lasted') stand and are strengthened.
suggested_fix: Compute every interval with quasi-Poisson (Pearson-scaled) or NB2-ML model-based errors, or with HC0 scaled by n/(n-k). Replace 'are correlated from month to month' with the residual diagnostics (Ljung-Box p >= 0.33), or drop it.

title: The 'sampling interval' measures the precision of a mean of two fixed metropolitan profiles, not of Spain's ratio; averaging made it narrower

title: Dual-carriageway ratio is above 1 only with a normal quantile; 'every road type' is fragile
disclosure_where: Not disclosed. The data.html technical notes and methodology.md section 9 say only that the road-type intervals are 'Poisson intervals widened by the square root of each road type's own dispersion across years (1.9 to 2.4)'. They name neither the quantile nor the 7 df. Table 1 prints 1.22 (1.02-1.47), so a reader can see the bound is close to 1, but not that it depends on z. By contrast, methodology.md section 4 explicitly switches to Student t in the same situation.
factual_core: factors.speed_severity_pooled widens each road type's pooled Poisson interval by the square root of a Pearson dispersion. That dispersion comes from a 16-row Poisson model (deaths ~ speed + C(year), 7 residual df), but the interval uses the normal quantile 1.96. With Student t(7), which the study's own rule prescribes when a scatter factor rests on few points, the dual-carriageway interval is 0.98-1.52 and includes 1. The speed page's heading 'More deaths per crash on every road type', the Figure 1 text 'Every interval lies above one' and the build guards all rest on that lower bound.
materiality: Table 1's dual-carriageway entry would read 1.22 (0.98-1.52) instead of 1.22 (1.02-1.47), and p would rise from 0.032 to 0.069. All four road-type intervals widen by 20.6% in log half-width. The other three types stay clearly above 1. Point estimates, the home-page range 1.2-5.9 and the 2.00 summary are unchanged. The heading and 'Every interval lies above one' would need to say the excess is clear on three road types and borderline on dual carriageways. Across reasonable constructions the dual lower bound is 0.98-1.03 (p 0.03-0.07), so the excess is borderline, not absent.
suggested_fix: Use t(df_resid) = t(7) (risk_trends.t_quantile) for the road-type intervals, or pool the dispersion across road types and use its df. Reword the heading (e.g. 'More deaths per crash on every road type, clearly on three') and the Figure 1 text. Restrict the guards at overview.py:171-173 and speed.py:76 to the three clear types. Note under Table 1 that on dual carriageways the 1.22 is not clearly separated from 1.

title: 2022 is pure model output; 2024 substitutes actual ITV readings where available

title: The 24-hour death definition misses late deaths unevenly between zones and crash types, shifting Catalan contrasts

Men are 84.6% of the 75+ drivers involved against 64.0% at 45–64, and within the same age men die about 2.3 times as often as women once involved. title: Committed GENERALISABILITY.md and model_metrics.json come from an undocumented re-render step, not from the README sequence

The committed files equal the documents() output, not the output of the README's `all` sequence, and the two differ.

Alternatively, end `all` with the documents step and list it in the README Reproduce block. Then regenerate GENERALISABILITY.md (0.708) and model_metrics.json.

title: Multiple rear-end collisions show 0 serious partly because serious multi-vehicle rear-ends are coded Encalç and merged into the single rear-end group
disclosure_where: The page and data.html disclose that 'Encalç' records the outcome, and merge it into rear-end collisions. For the multiple group, data.html#barcelona-crashes says the opposite: 'The 193 multiple rear-end collisions are a crash type of their own, and none had a serious or fatal injury.' Nowhere is it said that Encalç crashes include collisions of 3 or more vehicles.
factual_core: Figure 3 and the technical notes report that none of the 193 multiple rear-end collisions ('Abast multiple') was serious. Yet 7 of the 43 crashes coded with the outcome-linked term 'Encalç' involved 3-4 vehicles, and 4 of those were serious. The study maps every Encalç crash to the single 'rear-end collision' group, so the 0% for multiple rear-ends is partly produced by the outcome-dependent coding.
materiality: Under any grouping that does not depend on the outcome, Figure 3's multiple rear-end dot (now 0.0%, interval 0-2.0%) would sit at about 1.4-2.0%. The page's rear-end figure, '1.6% of 1,715', would become 1.4% of 1,708 (split by vehicle count) or 1.5% of 1,908 (all codes merged). The sentence 'none had a serious or fatal injury' misleads. No conclusion on the page changes: crashes in which a pedestrian was struck stay highest, and rear-end collisions stay below the 3.3% average (upper bound about 2.1%).
suggested_fix: Merge all three rear-end codes into one group in Figure 3 and the text (28 of 1,908, 1.5%). Alternatively, drop 'and none had a serious or fatal injury' and say that serious rear-end collisions of any number of vehicles were coded with the Catalan term, including 7 crashes of 3-4 vehicles.

title: Heading 'pedestrian struck ... most often serious' ranks point estimates that are not distinguishable from head-on collisions or falls inside a vehicle
disclosure_where: Figure 3, directly under the heading, plots every type with its n and 95% interval, so its overlap with head-on collisions and falls inside a vehicle is visible. The Encalç merge is explained in the paragraph under the figure and in data.html. Neither the heading nor the text says the top three types cannot be told apart.
factual_core: The heading 'Crashes in which a pedestrian was struck were most often serious' and the sentence 'the share is highest when a pedestrian was struck: 7.3%' rank 65/885 above head-on collisions (9/147 = 6.1%) and falls inside a vehicle (23/402 = 5.7%). The data cannot tell these apart (Fisher p = 0.73 and 0.34). The top place also depends on counting 'Encalç' (26/43) with rear-end collisions, which the page discloses.
materiality: No number changes. The heading and 'the share is highest' state an order among the top three types that the data cannot establish. What the data support is that these crashes were more often serious than average (lower bound 5.8% > 3.3%). 'More than twice the average' holds only for the point estimate (7.34% against 6.51%); the interval's lower end is 1.78 times the average.
suggested_fix: Change the heading to 'Crashes in which a pedestrian was struck were among the most often serious'. In the text, write '...7.3%, against 3.3% on average, though not distinguishable from head-on collisions (6.1% of 147) or falls inside a vehicle (5.7% of 402)'. Alternatively, use the superlative only when the same check as the 75+ claim passes.

title: Speed is the maximum of 17 eligible causes, quoted with a nominal interval; its rank over the runner-up is not established
disclosure_where: The cause paragraph of barcelona.html gives n = 38 and the per-group 95% interval right next to the claim. data.html Table 23 lists all 17 shares without intervals; the runner-up is 7.5% of 67. The downloadable CSV has each cause's interval. Nothing says that speed was picked as the largest of 17, or that the runner-up overlaps it. By contrast, catalonia.html qualifies its small top-ranked road type ('but from only N crashes, and its 95% interval overlaps').
factual_core: The page says 'a serious or fatal injury was most often recorded where excessive or inappropriate speed was: 18.4% of 38 crashes (95% interval 9.2–33.4%)'. That share is the largest of the 17 causes with at least 30 crashes, and the interval is an unadjusted per-group Wilson interval. Speed's share cannot be told apart from the runner-up (not giving way to the right, 5/67). A selection-adjusted interval is about 6.5–42%, still above the 3.3% average.
materiality: No published number changes. The above-average comparison survives selection: the Bonferroni lower bound is 6.5% > 3.3%, and p is about 0.0002–0.0006. What is not established is 'most often': p = 0.11 against the runner-up. The quoted interval also covers less than its nominal 95% for a group chosen as the maximum; adjusted, it is 6.5–42.3%. The fix is wording only.
suggested_fix: In site/regional.py page_barcelona, write: 'the highest share among causes recorded in at least 30 crashes was where excessive or inappropriate speed was recorded: 18.4% of 38 crashes (95% interval 9.2–33.4%), against 3.3% of all crashes; with so few crashes it cannot be told apart from the next, not giving way to the right (7.5% of 67)'. Alternatively, use 'most often' only when a _check shows the top cause's interval excludes the runner-up's share.

title: 'Six of the eight changes kept the same direction' counts interval agreement, not direction
disclosure_where: validation.html (validation.txt:24) states the correct criterion ('95% intervals on the same side of 1 in both periods') and gives run-off and heavy rain as the two whose interval includes 1 in a period. The model page's second clause ('should not be read as settled') is accurate.
factual_core: The model page says 'six of the eight changes below kept the same direction; the other two should not be read as settled'. The code (models.py:234-245) counts something else: both 95% intervals on the same side of 1. By point estimate, 7 of 8 kept their direction. 'Ran off the road' (1.17 and 1.95) did not reverse; only heavy rain did (0.63 vs 1.12).
materiality: Wording only, and conservative: it understates stability (7 of 8 kept direction). The heavy-vehicle contrast meets both criteria, so the heavy-vehicle finding is unaffected.
suggested_fix: Write 'six of the eight changes had 95% intervals on the same side of 1 in both periods' (or 'kept a clear direction').

title: 'The national records train no published model' is false: two published logistic regressions are fitted on them
disclosure_where: On the same page, sources.txt:50 says the national records describe Spain 'including the associations reported under Crash circumstances in Spain', and that they train reference and diagnostic models 'but no published predictive model'. data.txt:467 and severity.txt:41 say the regressions are fitted on DGT records and describe associations only.
factual_core: sources.txt:9 (sources.py:670) says 'The national records train no published model', yet the DGT crash records are the fitting data of two published association logistic regressions. Their odds ratios are on the severity page and their fitted probabilities in data Table 15, and they have a model card with decision KEEP. The same page's line 50 correctly says 'no published predictive model'.
materiality: Wording only: one missing word ('predictive') in the summary sentence. No number changes. The use of check-6-failing fields in the association models is already disclosed (severity.txt:41; data.txt:527-528 on alignment 'unknown' describing recording practice).
suggested_fix: At src/dgt_stats/site/sources.py:670, write 'The national records train no published predictive model, because provinces record several of their fields unevenly.'

title: 'Per 1,000 licence holders' means B-licence holders by age but licence holders of any class by sex
disclosure_where: The tool page does not define 'licence holders'. The any-class definition of the sex rates is only on data.html and in the driver_risk.py docstring.
factual_core: In the driver risk comparison tool, the age view's 'Involved in injury crashes, per 1,000 licence holders' (and killed per million licence holders) divides by B-licence holders. The sex view, under the identical label and scale, divides by holders of a licence of any class.
materiality: Ratios within each view are internally consistent. Comparing levels across views is not: for young drivers the gap is 2-4%, but at 75+ the same label covers denominators that differ by about 20%, so an all-sex 75+ rate exceeds both single-sex rates. The attacker's 'about 1-2%' understates the 75+ effect (12% on the ratio, 10-23% on levels), but no published sentence rests on comparing the two views.
suggested_fix: Label the sex view 'per 1,000 holders of any licence class' and the age view 'per 1,000 car (B) licence holders', or switch the sex view to B holders for 2022-2024 as proposed under F7-sex.any-class-denominator.

title: Driver comparison: per-km ratio between two non-reference ages shown without an interval; nested-group intervals computed as if independent
disclosure_where: The tool notes say only that per-km rates carry 95% sampling intervals. data.txt:80 says ratios of two rates carry log-normal intervals, and data.txt:286 says the per-km sampling intervals are probably too narrow. Nothing addresses nested pairs or the bare cross ratio.
factual_core: In the driver risk comparison, a per-km comparison of two non-reference age groups prints a ratio of the two point estimates with no interval. Pair ratios between nested groups (65+ against 65-74 or 75+) use a standard error that treats the counts as independent, although 65+ contains them, so those intervals are too wide.
materiality: Nested-pair intervals are 1.5-2.0 times too wide in SE. This is conservative: no displayed difference is overstated, and only one odd comparison (killed per involved, 65+ vs 65-74) wrongly looks inconclusive. The disjoint comparison that matters (65-74 vs 75+: 0.53, 0.38-0.75) uses the correct formula. The bare cross ratio of 1.10 has a true interval that spans 1, but both component intervals are printed in the same line, and the sentence calls it 'the estimate'.
suggested_fix: Give the cross-group per-km ratio an interval from the joint replicates, or say that it is not distinguishable from 1. For nested pairs, use Var(log ratio) = 1/x_small - 1/x_big (and the binomial analogue for deaths per driver involved), or do not offer 65+ against its own subgroups.

title: Trends explorer computes changes across known steps in recorded injury crashes without saying so
disclosure_where: data.html (steps at lines 125, 190, 706; recording dependence at line 78), trends.html line 43 (urban step), long-run.html line 24 (the split cannot be told from these series). The tool's notes only say 'as recorded by the police' and 'recorded injury crashes'. The tool page links to long-run.html and data.html#rates.
factual_core: The trends explorer computes percentage changes and average annual changes for injury-crash series, and for deaths per 100 crashes, across two steps that the site elsewhere calls steps in recorded crashes: 1997-1998 (+13.4%, +21.4% interurban) and urban 2013-2016 (+25.7% against -1.5% interurban). The tool's notes do not mention either step.
materiality: Every number the tool shows is correct. The defect is missing context. Any period that spans 1997-98 or 2013-16 mixes a recording step with real change. Example: urban +37.6% over 2012-16, of which +25.7% is the 2013-16 step, set against -1.5% interurban. The -78.1% in deaths per crash since 1993 includes the 1998 crash step of about -12%. No published finding of the site changes.
suggested_fix: Add one sentence to the notes for the crash indicators and for deaths per 100 crashes, for example: 'Recorded injury crashes step up 13% in 1998, and urban ones 26% in 2013-2016 (methodology); changes across those years mix recording with change on the roads.' Alternatively, mark 1998 and 2013-2016 on the chart.

title: The interurban fuel check is outside its range by only 4.9 deaths
disclosure_where: docs/methodology.md section 5: '2023 is 13 % above trend, just outside its range of ±12 %'. data.html long-run-interurban: '13% above their trend in 2023, against a range of ±12%'. long-run.html says only 'outside its range'. The page's 'at the edge' rule (EDGE=0.01 in long_run.py) covers only years just inside a range, never years just outside.
factual_core: Interurban deaths over national road fuel in 2023 were 1,288 against an upper bound of 1,283.1 (expected 1,140.6): a ratio of 1.1292 against 1.1249. The page calls this 'outside its range', but the margin is 4.9 deaths, and starting the segment a year later puts it inside.
materiality: Wording only. The verdict could equally read 'just outside' or 'at the edge'. The 8-point gap between the per-km ratio (1.049, inside) and the per-fuel ratio (1.129), which is the substance of 'the measures part', is unaffected.
suggested_fix: On long-run.html write 'just outside its range of ±12%', for example by applying the EDGE rule in _where/_cell to years outside a range by less than 1%.

title: Interval labelled 'for an ordinary year' is the interval of the change; 'every change lies inside its interval' is true by construction
disclosure_where: Figure 1 draws a dotted no-change line, and its alt text (not visible text) says 'Only the ratio for hospital admissions per tonne of road fuel has an interval that excludes no change'. The figure caption says 'intervals that allow for ordinary year-to-year variation'. data.html#trends-method, linked in the same sentence as the 1.5 factor, gives the factor's 0.6–8.7 interval, and the t5 widening already accounts for that uncertainty.
factual_core: Table 1's column '95% interval for an ordinary year' holds ratio × exp(±t5·sqrt(phi(1/y1+1/y0))), an interval centred on the observed change, not a range around no change. So 'Every change in deaths lies inside its interval' is true by construction. 'Had kilometres per tonne of fuel grown 0.3% a year faster than before' is a drift computed from zero growth since 2019 (1.01621^(1/5)-1), not one relative to an earlier pace. The dispersion's 0.57–8.7 interval is given only on the data page.
materiality: No verdict changes: the two readings are algebraically equivalent, since ratio ∈ exp(±s) exactly when 1 ∈ ratio·exp(±s). Three pieces of wording change: the column label; the sentence 'Every change in deaths lies inside its interval', which is vacuous and, read literally, would also class admissions per tonne as within; and 'faster than before', which should be 'from 2019'. On the long-run page, by contrast, 'faster than before' is correct because the trend carries the pre-2019 pace. The omitted dispersion interval is not a defect.
suggested_fix: Relabel the column '95% interval of the change, allowing for ordinary year-to-year variation'. Replace the sentence with 'Every interval for deaths includes no change'. Write 'had kilometres per tonne grown 0.3% a year since 2019'.

title: February 2020 comparisons include the leap day
disclosure_where: docs/methodology.md:384-385 says 'Deaths and fuel are monthly totals and are not adjusted for the number of days in a month', a few lines before the lockdown comparison, but in the context of the month effects. Neither the 2020 leap day nor any day-count note appears on data.html#seasons-lockdown, where '13% and 16%' are quoted, or in the Figure 3 caption.
factual_core: February 2020 had 29 days against 28 in each of 2017-2019. The February rows of the lockdown comparison (deaths, road fuel, petrol, all monthly totals) are therefore raised by 29/28, about 3.6%. The technical notes quote petrol in February 2020 as 16% higher, which per day is about 12%.
materiality: Technical notes: February petrol should read about 12% per day, not 16%, so January and February are equal rather than rising. Methodology range: '9 % to 16 %' becomes 9% to 13%. The Figure 3 February bars for deaths, fuel and petrol are shifted by about 3.6 points (deaths -3.5% vs -6.8% per day; fuel +5.1% vs +1.5%). The conclusion that petrol and toll traffic were already above baseline, so their April falls measured from that level would be larger, is unchanged. April, the month the page relies on, is unaffected.
suggested_fix: Compare February per day (petrol about 12% higher), or add 'February 2020 had 29 days' to the technical note and the Figure 3 caption; change the methodology range to '9 % to 13 %' per day.

title: Research conclusions, page docstring and sensitivity analysis still centre on Method A (2.53), not the published 2.68
disclosure_where: DRIVER_AGE_EXPOSURE.md:18-27 and data.html ('The alternatives below vary one choice at a time from the Barcelona-area survey's profile'). The docstring and the stale data.html glossary, rates paragraph and Table 7 caption are not flagged.

Every one-at-a-time alternative in risk_national_sensitivity.csv is built from Method A, so none exists around the published average. The drivers.py docstring promises a range the page no longer prints.
materiality: No published number changes and the ends of the range do not move. A few sentences on data.html describe the central method as the EMEF profile alone. It is a documentation inconsistency.

Update the DRIVER_AGE_EXPOSURE.md conclusions, the drivers.py docstring, data.py:268/286 and drivers.py:228 so that they name the averaged profile, and change data.py:1337 to match what the pages print.

title: Licence growth since 2018 lowers the central to about 2.16–2.23; the package's check uses all licence classes and wrongly says 2018 car licences by age are unavailable
disclosure_where: Methodology page, 75+ section: 'Some evidence points lower: licence holding at 75 and over has risen since 2018, more than at 65–74'. Its assumptions table: 'Rising licence holding since 2018 would lower the figure'. Both give the direction only. The size appears only in risk_older_reference_checks.csv (1.88, linked from the drivers page, with no note that it is on the Barcelona profile) and in DRIVER_AGE_EXPOSURE.md:806 (whose header says it works from Method A). The false statement about the 2018 tables is in that document and in the code comment.
factual_core: The package's cohort check scales Madrid's 75+/65-74 km ratios by the 2018-2024 change in licence holding of any class, and gets 1.88 on the Barcelona profile. It justifies this by saying (national.py:2152-2153, DRIVER_AGE_EXPOSURE.md:806) that the 2018 census tables give licences by age only for all classes together. The attacker says the 2018 tables list class combinations by age, that the car-licence (B) change is larger, and that the cohort-updated figure on the published average profile is 2.16 (car) or 2.23 (any class), against 2.43.
materiality: The published 2.43 (2.0–3.0) does not change: it is explicitly conditional on Madrid's 2018 pattern. The exploratory cohort-updated figure becomes 1.82 instead of 1.88 on the Barcelona profile (−11.4% instead of −8.4%), and 2.15 instead of 2.23 on the published average profile (−11.2% instead of −8.3% from 2.427). Both stay inside the sampling interval (unrounded lower end 1.965) and the range 0.97–3.20. The documentation sentence about the 2018 tables is false and should go.
suggested_fix: Derive the 2018 car-licence counts from P_6_1_2_7/P_6_1_3_7 (rows containing B, B+E, BTP, C*, D*). Recompute the cohort check on the published average profile (about 2.15) and label it as such in risk_older_reference_checks.csv. Delete the false sentence at national.py:2152-2153 and DRIVER_AGE_EXPOSURE.md:806.

title: The 3.4 ratio is printed without its 95% interval (2.6–4.5) on the home and drivers pages
disclosure_where: On the drivers page, Figure 2 (just below the deaths text) shows each rate's 95% interval, and the two do not overlap. The driver-risk tool, linked from both pages, prints the ratio with its interval. The data page says ratios of two rates carry log-normal intervals (data.txt:80). Nothing appears next to the claim on the home page.
factual_core: The 3.4 ratio appears in home finding 3 and in the drivers page's lead with no 95% interval, which is about 2.6–4.5. The home page gives intervals for two other main findings, and the drivers page body gives them for its other ratios. The ratio's interval is printed only in the driver-risk tool.
materiality: The number does not change: 3.4 (95% interval 2.6–4.5). Its lower end still supports 'far more likely', which the build guard checks. The reader is not told that the ratio, based on 71 deaths, is known only to about -24%/+32%.
suggested_fix: Write '3.4 times as often (95% interval 2.6–4.5)' on the home page and in the drivers page's lead.

title: The per-licence denominator counts any licence class against private-car drivers; B-holder counts exist for 2022 too
disclosure_where: data.html, 'Men and women': 'The licence holders are holders of any class of licence', with the B-licence effect quantified only for deaths per licence holder in 2023-2024 (3.49 to 3.57). Table 11's note says 'Licence holders include every type of licence'. docs/methodology.md and docs/research/STATISTICAL_AUDIT.md repeat the premise that B holders exist only in the text files. The drivers page claim and Figure 3 say only 'per licence holder'.
factual_core: The 2022-2024 private-car sex rates divide by holders of a licence of any class. The published census tables for 2021-2023 give B (car) licence holders by sex and age (Total censo minus 'Sin permiso grupo B'). With B holders as the denominator, the 18+ involvement ratio is 1.42 (1.41-1.43) instead of 1.39 (1.38-1.40), and the 75+ ratio is 1.60 instead of 1.43. So the methodology sentence 'The census gives car-licence holders by sex and age for 2023-2024 only' is inaccurate.
materiality: The headline involvement ratio would be 1.42 (1.41-1.43) instead of 1.39 (1.38-1.40), +2.4%, and the B-based value lies outside the published interval. Figure 3's 75+ involvement point would be 1.60 instead of 1.43 (+12%), which is not disclosed anywhere. Deaths per licence holder: 3.71 instead of 3.63. The direction is unchanged and the once-involved ratio (2.62) is unaffected. The stated reason for keeping any-class holders is factually wrong for 2022.
suggested_fix: Use B holders for the 2022-2024 pooled rates: 2022 and 2023 from the tables (Total censo minus 'Sin permiso grupo B'), 2024 from the text file. Keep any-class holders only for the 2014-2024 trend. Alternatively, give the B-holder ratios for involvement (1.42) and for the 75+ band (1.60), and correct the sentence to say the census tables give car-licence holders by sex and age from 2021.

title: The lede mixes years, and a module docstring is stale
disclosure_where: Same page: the 'Men and women' paragraph gives the same figure (2.62) with 'pooling 2022-2024', and Figure 3's title says 2022-2024. The lede itself gives no window. The docstring is internal and not published.
factual_core: The drivers-page lede, after 'in Spain in 2024', says 'men 2.6 times as often as women' once in a crash. That is the 2022-2024 pooled ratio (2.617); 2024 alone gives 2.89 (2.27-3.68). Separately, the docstring at driver_risk.py:21-23 says no file measures driving by sex and the sex rates are never per kilometre, which national.sex_per_km and the published risk_sex_per_km contradict.
materiality: The lede reads as 2.6 for 2024, while 2024 alone is 2.9 (about 10% higher). The 2024 interval (2.27-3.68) contains 2.6, and the pooled figure is the steadier estimate, so no conclusion changes. The stale docstring affects code documentation only.
suggested_fix: Write 'and, pooling 2022-2024, men 2.6 times as often as women', and update the driver_risk.py module docstring to point to national.sex_per_km for the per-km comparison.

title: The page's foreign-registration caveat names one direction; external data bound the net effect on 2.5 to roughly 2.2-2.85
disclosure_where: The page's limitation, next to the claim, gives only the counts side. The linked data.html note (vehicles.py:312-317) and docs/methodology.md:692-697 give both sides and say the direction is unknown.
factual_core: The vehicles page's limitation names only one side of the registration mismatch: foreign vehicles in the crash counts. It omits Spanish vehicles' kilometres driven abroad, which sit in the denominator. The net effect on '2.5 times per kilometre' is small and of uncertain sign.
materiality: About plus or minus 10-13% on the 2.5, with uncertain sign. It cannot touch the contrast between 10.3 per vehicle and 2.5 per km, or any ranking.
suggested_fix: Rewrite the page's sentence: 'The crash counts include foreign-registered vehicles, and the kilometres include Spanish vehicles' travel abroad; the two partly offset and the net direction is unknown, which bears most on heavy trucks and buses.'

title: The 18–29 inside-city km rest on 49 respondents; single EMEF years give 2.05–3.99
disclosure_where: The '(2-4)' print follows the rule stated on data.html under Table 7: ends are printed to a unit at least twice the larger Monte Carlo error. The clustering caveat is on data.html for the national intervals (Table 7 text and the 75+ section) but not beside Table 10. The 49 respondents appear only in docs/research/DRIVER_AGE_EXPOSURE.md:391-396 and 405-410.
factual_core: The 18-29 internal-trip kilometres rest on 49 EMEF respondents (96 trips; 13/16/20 by year). The top 5 respondents carry 36% of the weighted internal km, and 4 trips of 10-50 km straight-line carry 14%. Single years give internal-only ratios of 3.99/2.05/2.35. The interval 1.76-4.32 prints as '(2-4)'. data.html states neither the respondent count nor, beside Table 10, the clustering caveat.
materiality: The size of the young ratio (2.14-2.61) is imprecise, and the internal-only 2.61 moves to 2.42 under an alternative km treatment. The direction (above 1) is robust in the pooled data. The printed interval already signals the imprecision. Rounding 1.76 up to 2 slightly flatters the lower end. No conclusion changes.
suggested_fix: Beside Table 10, note the 49 young respondents and that the intervals treat respondents as independent. Print the 18-29 internal-trip interval as 1.8-4.3, or say that its lower end is below 2.

title: Only the numerator variant that raises the 65+ ratio is cited; the DGT-comparable refused-care variant lowers it
disclosure_where: data.html 'Definitions: Injury crash' (glossary on the same page, away from Table 10) says Barcelona counts people who refused medical care as slightly injured, while DGT's slight injury needs care. The combined variant (0.82-1.14) is in risk_barcelona_rates.csv, linked from drivers.html. Also docs/research/DRIVER_AGE_EXPOSURE.md:344-353 and 365-371, and docs/methodology.md:575-578.
factual_core: 459 of 6,851 injury crashes (6.7%) have only casualties who refused care, whom DGT would not count as injured. They hold 258 of the 3,321 working-day car drivers (65+ 9.9% against 45-64 6.9%). Leaving them out alone gives 65+ 0.776/1.076/0.909 and 18-29 2.59/2.21/2.13. The page cites only the on-duty variant, which raises the 65+ ratio.
materiality: About -0.03 on the 65+ ratio (0.80-1.11 becomes 0.78-1.08) and about -0.02 at 18-29, far inside every interval. No conclusion changes.
suggested_fix: Beside Table 10, note that the city's injury crashes include those where every casualty refused care, and that leaving them out gives 0.78-1.08 at 65 and over.

title: Table 24 places the city check beside the national transfer without saying it cannot confirm or bound the national ratio
disclosure_where: docs/methodology.md:578-582 and docs/research/DRIVER_AGE_EXPOSURE.md:339-342 and 351-353. Both are linked from data.html but not at Table 24 or the check. The page itself names the population ('inside Barcelona on working days', 'with no transfer').
factual_core: data.html (Table 24 and the opening of the check) never says that the Barcelona working-day figure is separate evidence about a different population and cannot confirm or bound the national 65+ ratio. Table 24 places 'Inside Barcelona on working days, with no transfer, the ratio at 65 and over is 0.80-1.11...' in the findings cell for the national transfer assumption.
materiality: This is framing only. The city figure is not used to adjust or bound the national estimate, and the 75+ paragraph reads the check cautiously ('neither confirms nor rules out'). A reader comparing 0.80-1.11 with the national 1.41 could still draw an unwarranted inference. The populations differ: city streets and ring roads against all roads, refused-care casualties, and traffic counted in the numerator only, which biases the city 65+ ratio down. Per I2, the more defensible city value is also about 1.1-1.16.
suggested_fix: End the Table 24 sentence with: 'separate evidence about a different population (city streets, a wider injury definition, traffic counted in the crashes only), which cannot confirm or bound the national ratio'.

title: 2023 left out, although DGT publishes its vehicle-km in the same release the manifest cites
disclosure_where: methodology.md:227 gives the 2023 car mean ('2023, 12,950 km'), and risk_km_crosscheck.csv gives the 2023 car_mean_km. So the car step (-0.9%, then -5.1%) is visible to a methods reader. data.html shows only 2022 and 2024, and does not give the all-vehicle total or the method change.
factual_core: DGT publishes 2023 vehicle-km by category in the same ZIP the manifest cites: TAB_05-KM_Veh-KM.xlsx, total 409.72 bn. The same figures appear in the 2024 report's Tabla 5 and the 2023 report's Tabla 9. The repository extracted only 4 of the ZIP's 17 xlsx tables. risk_km_crosscheck.csv leaves 2023 billion_km empty, and the code documents that vehicle-km 'need the fleet', which the repository lacks for 2023.
materiality: Including 2023 would show that the whole 2022-2024 fall comes in the step that crosses the method change. On its own, without I1's disclosure, a reader would see a step but not its cause. Its added harm beyond I1 is small.

title: An internal audit removed the correct caveat, and a test now forbids it

title: 'did not last' and the quoted 17-month interval rest on model intervals that placebos show are ~4× too narrow for the slope and the average

suggested_fix: Reword the heading, for example to 'A fall of about 7% around July 2006 whose size and persistence the series cannot pin down'. title: The 2014 urban baseline sits inside a step in recorded urban crashes that the per-series break rule cannot detect
disclosure_where: The factors page gives only a general caveat, in the section after Table 1: 'The rule finds discontinuities; it cannot say whether a break, or a trend within a run, comes from behaviour, from recording or from both.' The technical notes (data.html#factors-method) add: 'An unbroken run is not proof that recording stayed the same: the rule rules out only single-year jumps.' The specific urban step is documented only for other purposes: methodology.md:190-193 and 213-214 (crash intervals and the frequency/severity split), trends.html ('a step in recorded urban crashes widens their intervals') and data.html (Since 2019 notes and the assumptions table). Neither the factors summary, Table 1, the technical notes nor methodology §10 links the step to the factor shares.
factual_core: The urban factor shares are divided by the speed report's scoped urban injury-crash totals. Those totals rose 15.8% in 2015 while interurban crashes fell 4.2%, and the rise has the signature of added recording. The urban speed share fell 12.1% that year, about half of the published 2014–2023 fall of 24%. The per-series break rule cannot see a shared shock that lowered all four non-drug urban shares by about 10% in 2015. The factors page labels the urban speed and manoeuvre runs 'comparable 2014–2023' and does not mention the step.
materiality: The published numbers (4.1%→3.1%, −24%) are arithmetically right as recorded shares. The interurban fall (−23%) is unaffected, and the direction of the urban fall holds under every baseline. The size of the urban fall is what changes. Taken from after the step, or with the 2015 joint shock removed, the comparable urban speed fall is about −14% to −22% (endpoints from 2015 or 2016, the 2015–2023 trend, or bridging 2015). The published −24% is reached only by stretching the post-step trend back over nine years. So 'about a quarter on each kind of road' is the top of the plausible range for urban streets; 'about a sixth to a fifth' is more defensible. The 'Comparable years 2014–2023' label for urban speed and urban manoeuvres is not supported for the 2014 baseline. For manoeuvres the direction of the bias is ambiguous: the fall is smaller from 2015 and larger from 2016. This qualifies the finding; it does not overturn it.
suggested_fix: On the factors page, beside the summary sentence or Table 1, add: 'Recorded urban injury crashes rose 16% in 2015, mostly slight-injury crashes in provinces that began recording more of them, which lowered every urban share that year. From 2016 to 2023 recorded speed on urban streets fell 18%.' Alternatively, start the urban runs in 2016 (or 2015). Optionally add a joint-shock check to the break rule, such as the geometric mean of the factor ratios within a zone.

title: Crash-type odds ratios differ sharply between urban streets and interurban roads; the published ranking holds only on interurban roads

It would add that on urban streets a head-on collision has about 2.8 times the odds, and a run-off or object strike goes with a death about as strongly as a pedestrian struck. title: 'Ranked crashes no better than the shares' rests on one underpowered 3-month test; designs using all 12 months find a gain that passes the package's own rule

title: The owner-field exclusion depends on the outcome and varies by province and year; it produces the reported interurban province misses, and its disclosed effect hides province shifts that cancel out

title: Calculator's '95% confidence interval' is conditional on one model choice and a shrunken estimator, so it under-covers
disclosure_where: Calculator page notes: 'Its 95% interval covers only the uncertainty in the model's coefficients, not the differences between places and years' (tool_calculator.py:261). Severity-models Table 1 caption: 'The intervals cover the uncertainty of the model's coefficients only.' The rare_level warning: 'its interval does not show how few records there are'. The calculator report, linked from the page notes, says explicitly that the intervals do not reflect 'the uncertainty of the choices of penalty, specification, through-town rule and province intercepts' (docs/research/SEVERITY_CALCULATOR.md:389-391). The attacker missed this. Undercoverage from shrinkage bias is disclosed nowhere.
factual_core: The calculator's interval expit(x'b ± 1.96 sqrt(x'Vx)) uses a bootstrap covariance of the L2-penalised by_zone, C=0.1 coefficients. It ignores two things. First, the choice of specification and penalty: the choice was not decisive, and the runner-up specification moves estimates materially. Second, shrinkage bias: even when the model is true, its coverage of the model's own share falls below 95%.
materiality: For profiles like recorded crashes, a nominal 95% interval covers the model's own share about 92–94% of the time, a shortfall of 1–3 points; the default/reference crash is covered. For unusual combinations shown without warnings, coverage is about 85–90%, with roughly a sixth of them below 80%. Where specification uncertainty applies it is material: the runner-up specification moves a quarter of recorded profiles outside the interval (median 1.4 pp, p90 4.8 pp), and the reference crash from 13.4% to 10.9%. No published conclusion is reversed. The '95%' label is moderately anti-conservative, and it is conditional on the selected model, which the page only implies.
suggested_fix: On the calculator and model pages, say that the interval is conditional on the chosen specification and penalty. Then either widen it (penalised-Hessian/Bayesian covariance, or a bootstrap that repeats the whole selection) or state that it can under-cover for unusual combinations of inputs.

title: The 95% range behind "outside its range" leaves out the chance that the trend changes, and at 4-5 years ahead it is badly miscalibrated
disclosure_where: long-run.html, in the sentence before the claim, defines the range as 'where a year would be expected to fall had the trend's last segment gone on with its ordinary scatter'. The summary says 'an excess that depends on where the trend starts'. After Table 1 the page gives the 2013 start (10%/8%, at the edge / within) and says 'the two readings differ because the trend kept falling after 2019'. data.html (long-run-projections) says 'the trend asks whether the decline of 2011-2019 went on'. factual_core: The 'outside its range' verdict for deaths per tonne of fuel in 2023 and 2024 uses a 95% prediction interval around the 2011-2019 refit. The interval covers delta-method trend uncertainty and quasi-Poisson scatter with t(7), and it assumes the slope carries on. Applied to origins before 2020, the same method's ranges miss most years four to five years ahead. A smooth-trend model that lets the slope change puts both years inside.
materiality: The point excesses (+16%, +14%) do not change. 'Outside its range' and '(above)' stay literally true under the page's conditional definition, and the range covers about 94-97% when that condition holds. If the range also allowed for the trend changing course, as the smooth-trend model does, both years would read as within (upper bounds 1.334 and 1.455), and the heading's contrast with the count would weaken. Other structural or OLS forms keep them outside. The fix is a sentence of context, not a retraction.
suggested_fix: After 'outside its range' on long-run.html, add: 'The range assumes the 2011-2019 decline went on; it does not allow for the trend changing course, as it did in 2002 and 2011, and ranges built this way missed most pre-2020 years four to five years ahead.' title: The per-fuel 'beyond' rests on e-scooter (VMP) riders and motorcyclists, whose travel road fuel does not measure

The per-fuel numerator counts every casualty, so it includes VMP riders, whose travel burns no fuel. Give the per-tonne change without VMP and Otros (+8.8%, -2.6% to +21.5%, within) and for motor-vehicle occupants (+10.8%, +0.9% to +21.6%). title: Admissions verdicts are knife-edge: the scatter window, one dropped year or a multiplicity correction flips them
disclosure_where: The trends.html summary and section 2 call the count 'at the edge' and say the per-tonne excess would vanish with 0.3%/yr more km per tonne. data.html and methodology section 4 give the dispersion factors' chi-square intervals and the t5 widening. No page reports window, leave-one-year-out or multiplicity sensitivity.
factual_core: Under the published construction, admissions per tonne have t = 2.96 on 5 df (p = 0.031, lower bound +1.6%), and the count has p = 0.052 (lower bound -0.2%). This is the only 'beyond' among 13 rows. The verdicts flip with the scatter window, with dropping one year of 2013-2019, with the quantile, or under a multiplicity correction.

Across reasonable constructions its lower bound runs from about -1.8% to +3.9%, and after Holm over 13 rows it is not significant, so 'beyond it' in the summary should say just beyond or borderline. The alternatives most tied to admissions' own trend strengthen it rather than reverse it, so 'about half of equally defensible constructions reverse them' is overstated.
suggested_fix: Call the per-tonne excess borderline (lower bound +1.6%, p about 0.03 under the page's construction). Add one sentence on its sensitivity to the scatter window and to dropping a year, and do not single it out in the summary without that qualifier.

title: April 2020 'deaths per tonne of road fuel fell 24%' has no interval; the interval includes no change, and the figure moves with the baseline
disclosure_where: Not disclosed anywhere. site/seasons.html (heading, paragraph, Figure 3 caption and alt text), data.html#seasons-lockdown and docs/methodology.md lines 386-393 give point changes only. The same site prints intervals for comparable claims (seasons Figure 1 month effects; trends.html Table 1, where the per-tonne change from 2019 to 2024 is +3.5%, interval -6.7% to +14.9%). This section departs from that standard.
factual_core: The seasons page states the April 2020 per-tonne change ('deaths per tonne of road fuel fell 24%') and puts the falls in order in a heading (deaths fell more than road fuel and less than petrol or toll traffic). It gives no interval. With 40 deaths against a baseline of 375 over three Aprils, the 95% interval of the per-tonne ratio includes 1, and the size of the fall depends on the baseline and on applying the early-year adjustment only to petrol and toll.
materiality: No published number is wrong: -68%, -58%, -76%, -78% and -24% all reproduce. With a 95% interval of about -47% to +5% (exact) or -48% to +11% (the page's dispersion), the -24% per-tonne change cannot be told from no change (p 0.09-0.15). It is about 1.5 SD of ordinary April variation. The heading's 'deaths fell more than road fuel sold' is therefore not statistically established. 'Less than petrol or motorway traffic' is borderline on the plain baseline (p 0.03-0.12) and holds at p about 0.02 on the early-year reckoning the page itself uses. Across plausible baselines and adjustments the fall ranges from -15% to -28% and is always negative. The deaths fall itself (-68%, interval -53% to -78%) is robust.
suggested_fix: Add an interval and a qualifier to the paragraph, for example: 'so deaths per tonne of road fuel fell 24% (95% interval: a fall of 48% to a rise of 11%), within the variation of an ordinary April; against a 2019-only or a 2014-2019 baseline the fall is 15% or 28%.' Soften the fuel half of the heading, for example 'deaths fell about as much as traffic: by more than road fuel sold, a difference within chance, and less than petrol or motorway traffic'. Replace the sign-only guard at seasons.py:144-147 with one on the interval.

title: The per-tonne month pattern depends on how freight is weighted: 'February below' and 'August above' do not survive light-vehicle denominators
disclosure_where: The claims are labelled 'per tonne of fuel'. The lead adds 'but other measures of traffic disagree about August', and the section 2 heading 'The measures of traffic disagree about August, so the excess per kilometre is unknown' is next to the claim, but for August only. That fuel mixes freight with private travel is in methodology lines 369-370 and in trends.html#road-fuel, linked from section 2. Figure 2 shows the petrol and toll indices by month (February: deaths 84, fuel 91, petrol 85, toll 83), but the text never says February also depends on the measure. By singling out August, the page implies the rest of the pattern does not.
factual_core: Road fuel weights heavy vehicles above their share of kilometres, and heavy traffic has its own seasonality. As a result, the per-tonne month pattern depends on the freight weighting. With petrol, or with fuel net of a freight component, the intervals for February (and March under petrol) and for August include 1. July and September above, and April and May below, hold under every measure. The page warns about August only.
materiality: Every published per-tonne number and interval is correct. Read as risk per unit of traffic, which the lead invites by calling fuel 'the only monthly measure of traffic on all roads', February is as measure-dependent as August: below per fuel and diesel, null per petrol and per light fuel at s of 0.3 or more, above per toll. March is null per petrol. The robust part is April and May below, and July and September above. The heading 'February to May below it' holds per tonne, but February's reading per unit of traffic needs the same caveat August already has.
suggested_fix: After the August caveat, add: 'They disagree about February too: per tonne of petrol February is 0.99 times the average month (0.93-1.06) and per toll vehicle it is above it. April and May lie below, and July and September above, under fuel and petrol alike.' Optionally publish the per-petrol month effects beside the per-tonne ones.

title: Exposure comes from the two provinces with the lowest young licence holding in Spain; the package's own licence calibration, applied to both surveys, gives 2.37, outside the published interval
disclosure_where: data.html section on what the sensitivity range spans, and the assumptions row: 'gives 2.24, because young people in the province of Barcelona hold car licences less often than in Spain as a whole'; the regional profiles 1.64-3.63; the range 1.49-3.63. factual_core: The two source regions, the province of Barcelona and the Comunidad de Madrid, have the lowest ratio of young (18-29) to 45-64 car-licence holding among Spain's 52 provinces. The package's licence calibration (A2) applied to both surveys gives 2.37, below the printed interval. The within-EMEF urban gradient also points down. materiality: The central 2.68 is plausibly about 5-12% high. The symmetric licence calibration gives 2.37 (-11%), and scaling by the ECEPOV gradient gives about 2.37. The direction does not change, and every value lies inside the disclosed range. The attacker's '10-25%' and '2.0-2.4' rely partly on assumed urban weights.
suggested_fix: Add a symmetric licence-calibration row (2.37) to the sensitivity analysis and Table 9. State on data.html, and beside the estimate, that both source regions have Spain's lowest young licence holding and that the transfer probably overstates the 18-29 ratio. Consider showing the calibrated average beside 2.68.

title: 'Under other plausible assumptions it runs from 0.97 to 3.20' understates the upper side
disclosure_where: The methodology page says a sensitivity range 'is not a limit: assumptions not tested, or tested ones combined differently, could fall outside it' (glossary, and the 75+ section: 'not a limit, because the choices varied one at a time are not combined'). A roughly 5-7% care-home share of the 75+ population would move the central 2.43 to about 2.55-2.6, well inside its 2.0-3.0 interval.
