title: The heavy-truck multiples are the 2022 peak: 2023 and 2024 give 1.7 to 2.0 times per km and 7.9 to 8.3 times per vehicle
disclosure_where: On the page: - The lede says 'In 2022'. - The limitation says 'The kilometres are DGT's modelled estimates for 2022'. In the data.html vehicle notes (vehicles.py:307-311): 'DGT's later release gives mean kilometres by vehicle type for 2023 and 2024 on the same basis ... the vehicles page matches the crash tables and the kilometres for 2022 only.' docs/methodology.md:699-700: 'the comparison is made for 2022 only'. The general data.html section says that annual counts scatter more than Poisson chance allows. factual_core: The page's headline multiples for heavy trucks against cars (10.3 per vehicle, 2.5 per km, a fatal share 5.9 times a car's) come from 2022, the highest year in the series. 2023 and 2024, on DGT's same-basis kilometres, give lower values, and neither the page nor its notes says so.
materiality: On the fixed 2022 km, the headline '2.5 times per km' is 14% above the 2016-2024 pooled 2.20. With DGT's own km for each year it is 22% above the 2022-2024 pooled 2.05, and 25% and 45% above 2023 and 2024. '10.3 times per vehicle' is 14% above the nine-year pooled 9.0 and 24-30% above 2023-2024. The fatal-share ratio is 5.9 in 2022 against 4.3-5.5 in the other eight years. The ratios do not change direction in any year: - The per-vehicle excess is greater than the per-km excess, which is greater than 1. - Motorcycles rank first per km. - Heavy trucks' injury involvement per km is 0.38-0.42 of cars'. - Heavy-truck occupant deaths per fatal involvement are 0.16-0.18. So the story holds; the headline magnitudes are those of the high year.
suggested_fix: Print the per-km ratio with its interval and say that 2022 was the highest year. For example: '2.5 times per kilometre in 2022 (95% interval 2.2 to 2.9), the highest of 2016-2024; pooled over 2022-2024 with DGT's kilometres for each year, 2.0 (1.9 to 2.2)'. title: '0.80–1.11 under three versions' is narrower than the plausible treatments; Table 24 quotes it without caveat
disclosure_where: docs/research/DRIVER_AGE_EXPOSURE.md:379: 'Nor do they bound the ratios'. docs/methodology.md:578-580 says only that the versions do not bound the kilometres. data.html and Table 24 (src/dgt_stats/site/data.py:1340-1342) do not say it.

title: The leakage audit can only flag placeholder levels, so an outcome-coded ordinary level passes as 'safe'
disclosure_where: - data.html: 'The check for fields recorded differently when a crash was fatal looked only for placeholders rarer among fatal crashes, pooled over zones, and did not catch the road-owner field'. - barcelona.html and data.html: 'One crash-type code records the outcome rather than a kind of crash' (26 of 43). - validation.html, next to the person model: 'It uses the crash type as recorded, including a term the Guardia Urbana uses almost only for serious crashes ... part of its ranking may come from how serious crashes are coded'. - methodology.md:1270-1280: the check's limits, Encalç, and that the Barcelona models were fitted on the field as recorded and not refitted. Not updated: ML_LEAKAGE_AUDIT.md and ml_feature_catalogue.csv still say 'safe' with no caveat, and data.html's 'variables that encode the outcome enter none' is not qualified.
factual_core: The leakage audit's recording check compares only placeholder levels with the other rows, so it cannot flag an ordinary level that is used mainly when the outcome occurs. accident_type is therefore labelled 'safe' in both Barcelona feature tables, although its 'Encalç' level (rear collision while catching up) records the outcome.
materiality: No published number or headline changes: - The Barcelona crash model was replaced by a table, and the person model is research only, with the coding caveat printed next to it. - The published Catalan calculator is unaffected. The gap is in process and documentation. The audit's 'safe' label for accident_type is stale, and the check cannot detect this class of leak.
suggested_fix: Add a by-level scan to recording_check: the target share of every level against the rest, with a binomial test. Add a note to accident_type's catalogue reason that 'Encalç' records the outcome in the Barcelona tables. Qualify data.html's 'variables that encode the outcome enter none' for that level.

title: Urban speed ratio partly confounded by time of day; road-type labels inconsistent across pages
disclosure_where: data.html speed notes: 'autopistas to motorways, autovías to dual carriageways, the rest to other interurban roads; that match is checked only through the interurban total'. Methodology section 9 (codes 1-2, 3, rest; mapping not reconciled by road type). Methodology section 3: the speed comparison 'group[s] the raw codes differently'. Nothing on the speed page or home page. Time-of-day confounding is covered only by the generic 'associations ... not estimates of what speed causes' caveat.
factual_core: Two claims. (a) Hour x weekday composition explains part of the urban ratio: Mantel-Haenszel 4.84 over 168 strata and about 5.2 over 4 strata, against a crude 5.59. (b) The speed page's 'dual carriageways' are only DGT autovías (road code 3). Conventional dual-carriageway roads (code 5) sit in 'other interurban roads', and the long-run page counts autovías as motorways.
materiality: No published number changes. The code-3-only mapping is the one the report's own categories force (Autovía against Resto de vías interurbanas), so the ratios are matched correctly; only the English label is ambiguous and inconsistent across pages. 'Dual carriageway' is a common English rendering of autovía. Autovías are divided, access-limited roads that need not meet every autopista requirement, so 'motorway-standard' slightly overstates them. The time-of-day part lowers the urban ratio by about 13% (about 5.1 for 2016-2023), and it stays far above every interurban road type.
suggested_fix: Label the category 'autovías (dual carriageways with limited access)' on the speed page and home page. Add a note that conventional dual-carriageway roads are counted among other interurban roads, and that the explorer's road groups differ. Optionally report the hour x weekday-adjusted urban ratio.

title: 'Outside its range' for deaths per tonne of fuel in 2024 is conditional on the data-chosen 2011 turning point
disclosure_where: long-run.html: the summary says 'an excess that depends on where the trend starts', and the paragraph after Table 1 gives the 2013 start (10% and 8%, at the edge in 2023 and within the range in 2024). data.html long-run-projections has a 'last segment from 2013' row. methodology.md section 5 says the segment intervals 'take the turning points as known'. The 2012 start is not shown.
factual_core: The per-fuel projection range treats the data-chosen 2011 start of the last segment as known. The issue claims that allowing for the turning-point search widens the range enough to put 2024 (+14.3%) at the edge or inside, and that a start one year later (2012) already puts 2024 inside.
materiality: Ranges that allow for the turning-point search keep both years outside. The total half-widths grow 8-10% (dispersion 1.55) or 17-21% (2.8), not enough to flip 2024. The only flip is the one-year start shift: 2024 inside by 0.3 points. That is the same kind of sensitivity as the 2013 alternative the page already prints next to the claim.
suggested_fix: Optionally add that a trend started one year later, in 2012, already puts 2024 just inside its range. The ranges themselves need no change.

title: Several 'within / about the same / differ little' statements are low-power nulls read as near-equivalence
disclosure_where: (a) Intervals are printed beside the claim in Table 1 and Figure 1 of trends.html. (b) vehicles.html gives both rates and says 'the 95% intervals overlap', but Table 2 prints no intervals; they are only in q6_rates_2022.csv. The attacker's 'intervals are printed beside each' is therefore wrong for (b) and (c). No power statement appears anywhere.

(b) Heavy trucks have 'about the same rate per kilometre as cars' in occupant deaths: ratio 0.86 (0.64–1.14), from 51 and 681 deaths. (c) In Barcelona, 'Women and men differ little (1.8% and 1.6%)': ratio 1.18 (0.91–1.51).

(b) The sentence's purpose survives: the upper bound of the occupant-death ratio, 1.14, is far below the 2.5-times involvement ratio it is contrasted with. The page limitation also notes that foreign-registered trucks are in the counts but not the kilometres, which biases the truck rate up. (c) On the absolute scale the page uses throughout, the gap is under 1 point, against contrasts of 6.5% vs 0.06% and 5.3% vs 0.9–2.1% elsewhere on the page. Only a relative excess of up to about 50% is not excluded.
suggested_fix: (a) Add the width to the trends summary, as in the F2 low-power issue. (b) 'occupant deaths per km: 0.86 times a car's (95% interval 0.64–1.14), not distinguishable from cars'. (c) 'Women and men differ by under a point (1.8% and 1.6%; ratio 1.18, 0.91–1.51)'.

title: CI never regenerates most committed result tables, and its data-layer cache can go stale
disclosure_where: README.md:177-181 describes accurately what CI runs: data layers from the raw files, then pytest, no refit of the regional models or rerun of the validation, and tests that read the committed tables. ACCEPTANCE_REPORT.md:170 qualifies its claim with 'it regenerates'. The cache-key gap is undisclosed: the ci.yml comment says the cache is keyed 'on the code that reads them'.
factual_core: CI's regenerate-and-compare step covers only ingest, build_tables, model.py and five microdata steps. CI never runs analyse.py tables/figures/cards, emef.py, exposure_risk.py, severity_calculator.py or microdata models/validate. The data-layer cache key omits requirements.lock and src/dgt_stats/paths.py, among other imported modules, while ingest and build_tables skip existing outputs without --force.
materiality: There is no current staleness and no published number is affected. The risk is to the process: - A change to requirements.lock or paths.py would be tested against cached layers. - Drift in tables CI never regenerates can go unnoticed, as the thread-noise and documents-path mismatches in this batch did.
suggested_fix: Add requirements.lock and src/dgt_stats/paths.py (or all of src/dgt_stats/*.py) to the data-cache key, or run ingest and build_tables with --force on a cache miss of either. Add a scheduled full-rebuild job that runs analyse.py tables, emef.py all, exposure_risk.py all and the severity and microdata refits at a pinned thread count, then diffs reports/ and docs/.

title: Small gaps in the README's reproduce instructions
disclosure_where: The tests/test_site_browser.py docstring says the tests need 'a Chromium build; they skip otherwise'. The README itself says the withdrawn step's tables are committed and read by the model decisions. Nothing reconciles the README's '~2 min' for model.py with the script's own 'about fifteen minutes'.

(a) It implies `pip install -e .[browser]` enables the browser tests, but they also need a Chromium build, and CI pins playwright 1.56.0, which is not in the lock. (b) It labels `analyse.py withdrawn` optional, although the model decisions in `microdata.py all` need forecast_validation.csv. (c) Its step timings are shorter than observed.

title: Regional-model and model-review tables depend on the BLAS thread count, so the documented rebuild cannot reproduce them
disclosure_where: Thread dependence is explained only in code comments (scripts/emef.py:24-27, scripts/exposure_risk.py:25-27) for the distance model. docs/research/ACCEPTANCE_REPORT.md:170 and 267 mention 'solver noise' only for sev_*, and commit 862262d's message mentions it. docs/methodology.md §17 (lines 1208-1210) states the opposite, a 1e-4 tolerance. README.md:157-158 presents OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 as a load tip. The published data page makes no tolerance claim; it says only that one command sequence rebuilds everything, which is true.
factual_core: The lbfgs logistic fits (default tol=1e-4) in modelling.py:137, model_review.py:109 and dgt_audit.py:530 give results that depend on the BLAS/OpenMP thread count. scripts/microdata.py and scripts/severity_calculator.py do not pin threads. A clean rebuild at the README's suggested OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 therefore fails to reproduce 7 committed tables and 2 figures, and 95 cells exceed the 1e-4 relative tolerance that methodology §17 says was checked for this release.
materiality: No number printed on any page or in any generated document changes. All affected values agree at the 3 decimals printed, and the 2-3 GENERALISABILITY.md lines that changed come from the separate documents-path issue. Three of the seven tables are downloadable from the site: dgt_audit_artefacts, gen_calculator_transfer and ml_domain_strategies. They differ at the 5th-6th significant digit. The other four are only in the repository, so the claim that all seven are 'downloadable tables' is overstated. The false statement is methodology §17's 'checked for this release to a relative tolerance of 1e-4'. 95 cells exceed it: up to 4.7e-4 absolute on ROC-AUC, 0.008 absolute on calibration intercepts and 0.0047 on slopes, all in secondary diagnostic tables. One calibration-slope interval end crosses 1.0 (0.99983 -> 1.00014), but no sentence relies on it, and the build that checks interval sentences passed. The attacker's other two 'falsified' sentences hold: - 'every other fit is deterministic and needs no seed' is about random seeds, and the fits are deterministic at a fixed thread count, which I verified. - The 'last-bit differences between library versions' sentence concerns library versions, not optimiser stopping points.
suggested_fix: Fit the lbfgs logistic models with tol=1e-8, or solver='newton-cholesky' as severity_model.py already does, in modelling.py, model_review.py and dgt_audit.py. Also pin threads at the top of scripts/microdata.py and scripts/severity_calculator.py as emef.py does. Regenerate the seven tables. Restate methodology §17 so it gives the tolerance actually achieved and the thread setting used, or remove the 1e-4 claim.

title: Typed values from unarchived documents beyond the two declared exceptions, plus a transcription inconsistency
disclosure_where: The README (lines 11-15 and 101-119) and the data.html 'Reproducing the results' list name three categories: definitions, 'figures read from archived files', and two sets of measurements whose documents are not archived. The EMEF and km_itv values belong to the second category. EMEF_INVENTORY.md lines 133-140 describe the 15 reproduced 2024 figures, and line 57 says the executive summary is archived. The walking/transit ratio mismatch and the dead manifest reference are not disclosed anywhere.

The other claims: the distance.py docstring gives a walking road ratio of 1.32 and public transport 1.50, while ROAD_RATIO computes 1.40 and 1.49; and manifest.csv cites docs/phase3_plan.md, which does not exist.

Make the docstring and ROAD_RATIO agree on one walking and one transit ratio (1.32 and 1.50 if those are the report's ratios). Drop the docs/phase3_plan.md reference from manifest.csv.

title: Madrid city's junction coding in 2016-2018 is partly inconsistent, below the threshold of the inversion rule
disclosure_where: Madrid's 2016-2024 junction coding counts, including 2018's 2,052 and 928, are in the downloadable dgt_audit_junction_coding.csv, linked from sources.html 'Junction coding by province and year'. No text mentions them. The coding-breaks section on data.html says all four coding changes come from the Catalan provinces.
factual_core: The attacker makes four claims. Madrid city's junction coding is partly inconsistent: in 2018, 2,052 of 6,936 junction-flagged crashes have junction type 999 and 928 of 9,678 away-flagged crashes carry a junction type. In 2016-2018 the share of rear-end collisions flagged at a junction is 52.7/38.7/45.1%, against 29-32% later. Madrid's urban crude junction odds ratio (OR) is 0.78/1.21/0.91, against 0.54-0.78 in other years. The inversion rule detects only majority inversions, and the anomaly may pull the 2016-2018 yearly ORs slightly towards 1.
materiality: The pooled junction OR stays 0.69 (0.65-0.73); it moves by 0.002. The data.html sentence 'The junction odds ratio lies between 0.63 and 0.79 in every year' would read 0.61-0.79. The conclusion that the junction term does not vary between years beyond chance still holds (p = 0.16). Dropping Madrid moves 2017 and 2018 down by 0.01-0.02, so Madrid pulled them towards 1, but it moves 2016 the other way.
suggested_fix: Add one sentence to the coding-breaks section: Madrid city's 2018 records carry 2,052 junction crashes with no junction type and 928 away crashes with one, and dropping Madrid 2016-2018 moves the junction OR from 0.690 to 0.688 and the yearly range to 0.61-0.79.

title: The 482 checks test totals and the parser's own consistency; the predictor codes and most analysed inputs are not reconciled
disclosure_where: Directly after the 482 sentence, data.html 'Checks on the data' lists the identifier and dictionary checks, the per-year totals, province and month for 2024 only, deaths and vehicles by type, the speed-report provinces, and the census and driver tables, and links the full table. docs/methodology.md section 2 tabulates every check and tolerance. It also says CORES, Ministry km and km by owner age are checked in their readers, and INE, ITV and the speed report by unit tests. Section 9 states that the speed road-type mapping is not reconciled. The README and DATA_CONTRACT.md ('reconciled with the yearbook by 482 checks') carry only the summary sentence.
factual_core: The attacker splits the 482 validate.py checks into 64 internal checks, 123 comparisons between published tables and 295 comparisons of microdata with published totals. They say the checks do not reconcile: the severity-model predictor code distributions with DGT's 2024 tables; 2016-2023 province totals; the 2024 census used by the rates; or the speed report road-type numerators and the CORES/km/INE/regional inputs. They also say code_domain admits 999/998 in every column, and that '482 checks tie ... to DGT's published totals' implies coverage the checks lack.
materiality: No published number changes: every gap filled reconciles exactly or within one crash. The only defect is wording. In the README and DATA_CONTRACT summary sentences, 31 checks (6%) are purely internal and 33 (7%) compare codes with the dictionary rather than with published totals. The 26% that compare yearbook and census tables with published totals is exactly what the page and README say they do.
suggested_fix: Word the README and DATA_CONTRACT sentence as '482 checks, most tying the records and tables to DGT's published totals, the rest checking identifiers, codes and table consistency'. Optionally add the 2024 code-distribution and 2016-2024 province-year reconciliations to validate.py, since they pass.

title: 61% of the interurban alcohol rise falls in the two years other series broke; only 2016 is disclosed
disclosure_where: factors.html, next to the claim (factors.py:249-256): 'The interurban alcohol series has no break, but its share rose 11% in 2016, the year other series broke, and a further 30% from 2016 to 2023', and 'More recorded alcohol can reflect more drinking drivers, more breath tests after crashes, or both; these data cannot separate them.' The same section carries the general caveat that a trend within a run may come from recording. methodology.md §10 repeats the 2016 point. The 2019 coincidence and the interurban driver-table change in 2016 are not mentioned.
factual_core: The interurban alcohol share's two largest yearly rises are 2019 (×1.154) and 2016 (×1.110). Together they make up 60.9% of the 2014–2023 log rise (+50%). Urban distraction broke in 2016 and 2019, and urban alcohol in 2016. The page flags only 2016. In 2016 the interurban driver tables' unknown speed status went from 17.4% to 40.0%, and their unknown driver infractions roughly tripled. Treating the break years as artefacts gives a comparable rise of +17% to +35%.
materiality: The 2016 part is already disclosed beside the claim, and the page gives the post-2016 rise (+30%), which lies inside the attacker's +17% to +35% range. The undisclosed part is 2019. Only if the whole 2019 rise were an artefact would the rise read +13% for 2016–2023 (+17% for 2014–2023). There is no evidence for that: urban alcohol fell in 2019, the other interurban factors and the interurban driver-table unknown share did not move, and the only 2019 break is a fall in a different factor (distraction) in a different zone. 'Recorded interurban alcohol rose' survives every bridging. Mentioning 2019 would be a small consistency improvement; the published numbers stay.
suggested_fix: Optionally add one clause after the 2016 sentence: 'its largest single-year rise, 15% in 2019, came in the year urban distraction broke, though no other interurban series moved then.' Do not replace the +50% with a bridged range, which would assume without evidence that the 2019 rise is an artefact.

title: The break thresholds were validated against breaks seen by eye; the history cannot show they were fixed beforehand

Technical notes (data.html): 'The threshold is a convention, and every change is published with its test so that another threshold can be applied'. factors.html: 'A fixed rule'. Every other Table 1 run is the same for any threshold from 1.2235 to 1.5744 and any minimum count from 25 to 640, so no post-hoc choice within that range could have shaped them. 1.25 is a round value, and nothing suggests it was tuned to keep the manoeuvres run whole.
suggested_fix: Add to the technical notes: 'Runs are unchanged for thresholds from 1.2235 to 1.574 and minimum counts up to 640. Below 1.2235 interurban illegal manoeuvres breaks in 2017; below 1.159 interurban alcohol and urban speed split.'

title: 'as crashes shifted to urban streets' attributes to a real shift a change in the crash mix that is mostly a one-year recording step
disclosure_where: Not on factors.html, in its technical notes or in methodology §10. The urban step itself is described elsewhere (methodology.md §4, trends.html, data.html Since 2019 notes) for other analyses, but it is not connected to the mix explanation.
factual_core: The interurban share of the report's injury crashes fell from 40.6% (2014) to 34.2% (2023). 70% of that move happened between 2014 and 2015, the year the urban denominator rose 15.8%, largely through added recording. The page explains the larger all-roads fall in the speed share 'as crashes shifted to urban streets' and does not say that the shift is mostly in what was recorded. Measured from 2015 or 2016, the mix accounts for 10–12% of the all-roads fall rather than 23%.
materiality: No published number changes: 10.0%→6.9%, the counterfactual 7.6% and the within-zone falls are all correct. Only the parenthetical's mechanism changes. It should read 'the recorded mix moved towards urban streets', and most of that move was the 2015 step, which the evidence indicates is mostly added recording rather than a change in where crashes happen. The summary already leads with the within-zone falls, so a reader's conclusion about recorded speed is unaffected.
suggested_fix: Replace 'as crashes shifted to urban streets' with 'as the recorded mix moved towards urban streets, mostly in 2015 when more urban crashes began to be recorded'. Make the same change in the technical notes (factors.py:370-371) and methodology.md:766.

title: Relative changes are endpoint ratios with no uncertainty, although year-to-year scatter far exceeds chance
disclosure_where: The table caption says the values are 'at the start and end of every run', so the endpoint method is visible. No page or technical note mentions year-to-year scatter or gives any interval for factor shares.
factual_core: Table 1's relative changes are ratios of the last-year to the first-year share, with no interval and no trend estimate. Within each run the shares scatter around a log-linear trend at 2.3-140 times binomial variance. Endpoint and trend estimates differ, notably for illegal manoeuvres.
materiality: No direction stated in the text changes. The lead's fall in recorded speed of 'about a quarter' and the rise in recorded alcohol hold, with overdispersed trend intervals that exclude zero. Endpoint choice moves the two manoeuvres rows: urban -10% against -20% on trend, interurban +49% against +33%. The two distraction rows (+6%, +12%) lie within the year-to-year scatter, which the table does not signal. The text does not read them as rises; interurban distraction 'stayed between 24.8% and 28.8%'.
suggested_fix: Add a within-run trend in share with a quasi-binomial interval beside each Table 1 row, or add a note that year-to-year scatter is several times binomial, so changes of less than about 15% (the distraction rows) cannot be told apart from it.

title: Province-clustered (CR1) intervals understate the uncertainty of location contrasts carried by a few provinces
disclosure_where: The Table 1 caption says only '95% intervals clustered by province'. The model card limitation says 'Standard errors are clustered by province; with 4 provinces removed the clustering changes too.' Nothing mentions the small number or unequal size of the clusters.
factual_core: With 52 province clusters of very unequal size, CR1 intervals understate the uncertainty of contrasts that rest on a few provinces. Under a delete-one-province jackknife, two Table 1 intervals would include 1.
materiality: Under the exact jackknife, one of the nine Table 1 rows (urban motorway or dual carriageway / dual carriageway, 2.89) cannot be told apart from 1, not two. Interurban intervals are about 20% wider on the log scale, but every lower bound stays above 3.8. The headline crash-type, junction and wet intervals are essentially unchanged, and no sentence in the text depends on the affected row.
suggested_fix: Report CR3 (jackknife) or wild-cluster-bootstrap intervals for Table 1, or footnote the urban motorway / dual carriageway row as resting on 24 deaths in a few provinces, mostly Madrid.

title: 'Lleida in every year' rests on a 2010 lead of 0.6 per 100,000 (p = 0.46), and DGT's own provincial split for 2010 would put Girona first
disclosure_where: The page gives no uncertainty for the yearly ranking. The caveat next to the claim (crashes counted where they happen, residents where they live) concerns the denominator, not chance. The comment at regional.py:273 about chance variation is in the code only, not published.
factual_core: The file's per-resident rate is highest in Lleida in all 14 years. In 2010 the lead over Girona is only 0.57 per 100,000 (about 2.5 crashes, within chance), and the lead is also within chance in 2018, 2020 and 2022. DGT's yearbook splits 2010-2011 casualties among the Catalan provinces differently (with the same totals), and rescaling on that split would put Girona first in 2010.
materiality: Nothing published changes, and the sentence describes the file correctly. Fourteen wins out of 14 is itself strong evidence of a consistent difference, and the heading uses the pooled ranking, which is overwhelming. The DGT-split argument rests on a provincial assignment of unknown basis that differs only in 2010-2011, while the file assigns crashes by municipal province, the appropriate geography. Also, the sentence is about the file's crashes. At most, 2010 deserves 'narrowly'.
suggested_fix: '... most frequent in the province of Lleida in every year, though only narrowly in 2010 (42.1 against Girona's 41.5)'.

title: The fatal share does not keep rising above 60-70 km/h; the monotone pattern is mostly produced by the bands
disclosure_where: Directly below the sentence, Figure 3 shows each band with its 95% interval, and the top three intervals overlap. The text adds 'Higher limits are posted on faster, mostly interurban roads, so the rise describes the roads as much as the limits.' The plateau above about 70 km/h is not mentioned anywhere: not on the page, in methodology.md or in SEVERITY_CALCULATOR.md. CLAIM_LEDGER ledger-C|75 checked only that the bands are monotone.
factual_core: Among crashes with a posted limit, the fatal share climbs from 10-30 km/h to about 70 km/h and then stays flat at about 22-24% up to 120 km/h. The published sentence 'rises with it, from 7.4% at 10-30 km/h to 23.9% at 100-120 km/h' therefore implies a rise across the whole range that the data show only up to about 70 km/h.
materiality: No published number changes. The end points (7.4%, 23.9%) and the monotone band series checked at regional.py:254-258 are correct. The shape changes: the share is about 22-24% at every limit from 70 to 120 km/h, so 80-90 against 100-120 (21.8% vs 23.9%) is not a demonstrated step. The attacker's 'pairing 60 with 70 makes the series monotone' is weak. Split, the series dips only 0.6 pp (22.4% at 70 vs 21.8% at 80-90), well within noise, and pairing limits in tens is a natural choice (catalonia.py:73-79). The wording mildly overstates the shape; it is not an error.
suggested_fix: Replace the clause with: 'the fatal share rises with it up to about 70 km/h, from 7.4% at 10–30 km/h, and stays at 22–24% from 70 to 120 km/h'. Optionally give the per-limit shares in the technical notes.

title: The 1,351 people with no recorded outcome cannot be seriously hurt; leaving them out inflates every group share (direction-preserving)
disclosure_where: Next to the claim, the denominator is defined: the barcelona.html summary says 'Of the 15,848 people whose outcome was recorded', and the Figure 1 and 2 captions say 'as a share of the people in recorded crashes with a recorded injury outcome'. data.html#barcelona-people says 'They leave out the 1,351 people whose outcome was not recorded ... Counted as uninjured, the people without a recorded outcome would lower the overall share from 1.6% to 1.5%'. That covers the overall share only: no group figures, and the crash-file reconciliation is not used. DATA_QUALITY_MICRODATA.md:88 says 'a blank is not recorded, never uninjured'.
factual_core: The crash file's death and serious-injury counts equal those of the recorded people in every crash. So the 1,351 people with a blank outcome cannot be seriously hurt: at most 4 of them could be minor victims, and the rest are not victims. Leaving them out of the denominators raises each group's serious-or-fatal share, by an amount that differs by group.
materiality: Printed figures that would change if the blanks were counted: - summary: 1.6% -> 1.5%, pedestrians 6.5% -> 6.3%, motorcyclists 3.3% -> 3.1% - riders: cyclists 1.3% -> 1.2%, moped riders 2.2% -> 2.0%, personal mobility vehicle riders 2.1% -> 1.9% - men: 1.6% -> 1.5% - Table 20 heavy-truck drivers: 0.6% -> 0.5% Car drivers stay at 0.06% (3 of 5,200). No ranking, page check or stated contrast changes, and contrasts with car drivers grow slightly. The quoted figures move by 0.0-0.2 points.
suggested_fix: On data.html#barcelona-people, add one sentence: the crash file's serious and fatal counts match the recorded people in every crash, so the 1,351 people without a recorded outcome were not seriously hurt; counted in, the shares are 6.3% for pedestrians, 3.1% for motorcyclists, 0.06% for car drivers and 1.5% overall. Optionally add an all-people column to Table 20.

title: Home page gives a ratio from one reference crash, and its coefficient-only interval, as a general 'other circumstances held equal' effect
disclosure_where: severity-models.html, next to the model-page version of the claim: the paragraph 'Starting from a typical crash on a regional road and changing one thing at a time...', the Table 1 caption (the full reference crash) and 'The intervals cover the uncertainty of the model's coefficients only'. docs/research/SEVERITY_CALCULATOR.md:335-347 (the calculator report, linked from calculator.html and validation.html) says the same change can carry different ratios on the two kinds of road and gives urban x2.55. index.html neither names the reference nor says 'on average'.
factual_core: The home page's '2.0 times (95% interval 1.7–2.2), other recorded circumstances held equal' is the ratio of predicted fatal shares at a single interurban reference crash with a 13.4% baseline, and its interval is a coefficient-only delta-method interval for that one contrast. In the by_zone logistic model this probability ratio changes with the baseline and the zone, and the home page does not name the reference.
materiality: Small. Read as an adjusted average, the published number and interval hold: - standardised over all crashes, 1.97 (1.79–2.16), which would print as 2.0 (1.8–2.2); - over heavy-vehicle crashes, 1.89 (1.72–2.07), which would print as 1.9 (1.7–2.1). 'About twice' is unchanged. What is missing is a word on heterogeneity: about 2.4–2.55 on urban streets in the published model, and about 1.4–1.8 where the baseline is high or in the other provinces. This is a wording issue on a summary page, not a wrong number.
suggested_fix: On index.html, say 'on average' or name the reference ('for a typical interurban collision on a regional road'), or quote the standardised average (2.0, 1.8–2.2, over all crashes). Optionally add that the multiplier is smaller where the baseline is already high.

title: 'All ten groups inside' and the inside/outside verdicts by subgroup rest on razor-thin margins
disclosure_where: - validation.html prints the slope (1.03) next to the ten-group sentence and states the inside/outside rule for the subgroup lists. - Figure 1 on severity-models.html plots each group's 95% interval. - docs/research/SEVERITY_CALCULATOR.md:219 gives group 9 (21.9% vs 24.2%, 21.8-26.7%). - The site gives no margins, no HL test and no slope interval.

Group 9's mean estimate (21.906%) clears the Wilson lower bound (21.827%) by 0.08 points, and resampling or a defensible modelling variant gives 9 of 10. In the province x zone check, Barcelona interurban passes by 0.006 points despite an 11% overestimate.

suggested_fix: Next to the ten-group sentence, add the calibration slope's interval (about 0.97-1.11) and the HL p-value (0.28), and note that group 9 lies 0.08 points inside its interval. title: 'No choice saw the year it predicts' covers the four nested settings, not the options offered, the exclusion or the recodes

With every choice nested it is 0.74'). docs/research/SEVERITY_CALCULATOR.md:133-135 (province intercepts added after the 2016-2023 province calibration was examined) and :35-39 (earlier version with the artefact roads, 0.772). Neither the exclusion's use of all years nor the origin of the province option is mentioned next to the claim.

title: 'On urban streets in Barcelona' reads as the city, where the estimate was close; the miss is in the rest of the province
disclosure_where: The sentence's link ('the figures') goes to validation.html#later-years, which says 'urban streets in the province of Barcelona'. It also says 'in Barcelona city they were close (8.1% against 8.5%)' and that urban streets outside the city ran high (7.1% vs 6.0%, for all of Catalonia). SEVERITY_CALCULATOR.md gives the same split. The severity-models sentence itself does not.

Within that cell, Barcelona city is close: 8.10% vs 8.50% (7.19-10.02%), n=1,494. The rest of the province runs high: 7.28% vs 5.86% (5.10-6.73%), n=3,192, +24% relative.
materiality: No number changes. The issue is wording only: - Read as the city, the sentence over-warns Barcelona city users, whose estimate was close. - It can also leave users elsewhere in the province unaware that their estimates run about 24% high. - Read under the page's own convention (provinces named alone, as with Girona and Tarragona; 'Barcelona city' used elsewhere for the city), it is literally correct.
suggested_fix: Write 'on urban streets in the province of Barcelona (where estimates ran high outside the city; in the city itself they were close)'.

title: The 0.02-0.04 lead and 'ahead in every year' are measured against the weakest table; one extra column halves the lead
disclosure_where: The comparator is named and the gain is hedged: - severity-models.html, next to the claim: 'A table of fatal shares by road and crash type separates them less (27% and 4%): the gain is real but modest.' - validation.html: 'against 0.71 for a table of fatal shares by road and crash type', two sections after the 'lead is 0.02-0.04 ... ahead in every year' sentence, which says only 'the table'. - data.html calls it 'a table fixed before the test'. - rules.py declares the table in advance as the one 'a descriptive analysis would lead with'. - SEVERITY_CALCULATOR.md item 7 lists what the table ignores, including 'the road users involved'. No richer benchmark is reported, and nowhere is it said how much the lead depends on the table's richness.
factual_core: The published benchmark is a two-variable table (fatal share by road x crash type, pseudo-count 20, fitted on the same years as the model). Against it the nested model leads by 0.0305 (0.020-0.040) and is ahead in all 8 years. Adding the heavy-vehicle flag to the table halves the lead to about 0.015, and the model is then ahead in 6 of 8 years. An untuned main-effects logistic regression ranks as well as the tuned nested model.
materiality: No published number is wrong. 0.74 vs 0.71, the lead of 0.02-0.04 and 'ahead in every year' are all correct for the named comparator, which was declared in advance. Against a three-variable table the sentence would read 'lead about 0.01-0.02, ahead in six of the eight years'. 'Sorted crashes better than a simple table' still holds, because the interval excludes 0. Under the site's own keep rule (data.html: gain of at least 0.02), the heavy-flag table would leave the model below the bar (0.0146). That rule, however, specifies a table fixed before the test, and the heavy flag was chosen after seeing full-data results.
suggested_fix: In validation.html's lead sentence, write 'over a two-variable table of road and crash type'. Add one line giving the lead over the table with the heavy-vehicle flag (about 0.015, 95% 0.006-0.024; ahead in six of eight years), or over an untuned main-effects logistic regression.

title: The outcome-linked rear-end code inflates both scores and narrows the model's margin over the table
disclosure_where: barcelona.html, next to the claim (barcelona.txt:26-27): the code is described with its counts, and 'model and shares alike read the crash type as recorded, the code above included'. docs/methodology.md:1275-1281 says the Barcelona source models were fitted on the field as recorded and not refitted. The size of the effect on the AUCs is not stated anywhere. validation.txt:63 notes the code for the person model only. The model card's 0.737 carries no note.

The attacker says this inflates both AUCs by about 0.07-0.09 and tilts the comparison towards the table, so that with the code merged the model's gain rises to about +0.03. It also says validation Table 1's 'ranking held' entries for the crash model rest partly on the code.

Validation Table 1 verdicts do not change. What is inflated is the documented crash-model AUC in the generated docs (0.737, of which about 0.067 comes from the code) and the table's 0.734 (about 0.048). These are not printed on the site, and the model is removed.
suggested_fix: Add one line to docs/models/barcelona_crash_severity.md and to the validation note: 'with the Catalan rear-end term merged into rear-end collisions the model scores 0.670 and the table 0.686 on the same test rows (gain -0.016, 95% interval -0.07 to +0.05)'.

title: 'Too unevenly recorded to train a predictive model' overstates a file-level all-or-nothing rule; check 7's failure is confounded by province
disclosure_where: sources.txt:47-49, next to the claim on the sources page: 8 of 18 field groups fail check 6; NUDO, TIPO_VIA and fog/wind have coding breaks; check 7 fails 'only by four percentage points' and 'the decision does not rest on that narrow result'. sources.txt:50: the national records 'train reference and diagnostic models for those tests'. validation.txt:50 and 53: weather is unspecified in 6.1% of the test crashes. data.txt:524: the association regression ranks held-out years at 0.80, and 0.78 with missing levels folded. Not disclosed: the province spread of weather and surface inside the transfer population, and that no model restricted to the passing fields was tried. data.txt:467 and severity.txt:41 give the reason in its broad form and only link to the detail.
factual_core: Check 6 fails on specific fields: 10 of 30 pass. A national model on the passing fields ranks 30-day deaths at about AUC 0.81. Check 7's 54% share falls below 50% once province or field applicability is controlled. The transfer test uses weather and surface, and both fail the check-6 criterion inside the test population. So the summary 'its fields are recorded too unevenly between provinces to train a predictive model' says more than the audit shows.
materiality: No published number changes, and the decision not to publish a national predictive model stands. Controlling check 7 for province or applicability moves the share from 54.2% to 48.0% or 48.2%, with an interval spanning 50%. It is borderline under every specification, and the page already says the decision does not rest on it. Most of the 10 'comparable' fields carry disclosed coding breaks or are structural, so the attacker's 'recorded comparably' overstates. What remains is wording: 'its fields' should be 'several of its fields'. The use of weather and surface in the test is consistent with the stated rule (external test and reference models only), but the rule's cross-source validation covers Catalonia only.
suggested_fix: At data.txt:467 and severity.txt:41, write 'several of its fields (8 of 18 audited, including weather, surface, alignment and the junction fields) are recorded too unevenly between provinces, and others are coded differently in the Catalan provinces, so the project trains no national predictive model'. State that a model restricted to the evenly recorded fields was not tried. In the validation page's variables paragraph, add that weather is unspecified in 0% to 31% of test crashes by province.

title: 'The person model can only rank people' rests on one run's calibration slope, which the project's own review says varies from 0.63 to 0.91
disclosure_where: docs/research/ML_MODEL_REVIEW.md:54-56 ('its calibration slope varies between runs (0.63 to 0.91), and its Brier skill is 0.027: its probabilities stay close to the 1.4% base rate'). The site shows no probability from it, and in either fit the probabilities stay near the base rate. At most the wording 'can only rank people, not give probabilities' could become 'its probabilities failed the pre-declared calibration check (slope 0.63; 0.91 in a differently regularised refit)'.

title: 'Criteria fixed in advance' / 'set before any result was read' cannot be verified from the repository
