title: The direction of the harmonised model's calibration-slope miss depends on the estimator, and the documents report different ones
disclosure_where: GENERALISABILITY.md:135-136, linked from validation.html, lists both estimators with slopes 1.037 and 0.923. The validation Table 2 note says each model uses the method chosen on its own validation data. DGT_MICRODATA_AUDIT.md (and its copy at GENERALISABILITY.md:330) gives the logistic numbers without naming the estimator.
factual_core: For the same national transfer test, the validation page reports calibration slope 0.92 and mean estimate 14.5% (boosted trees). The DGT microdata audit reports slope 1.04 and mean predicted 14.2% (logistic regression) without naming the estimator. Below and above 1 differ in direction, so whether the estimates are 'a little more extreme than the outcomes warrant' depends on the estimator.
materiality: The validation page's 0.92, 14.5% and 'a little more extreme' are correct for the published (boosted-trees) harmonised model. The audit doc's figures belong to the logistic variant, and its gap mixes estimators (-0.012 vs a like-for-like -0.011). 'Close to calibrated overall' holds for both estimators, and both pass the study's 0.8-1.25 slope rule. Only the audit document's labelling is inconsistent.
suggested_fix: In dgt_audit.transfer_checks, select the chosen estimator from ml_selected (as validation.py does) instead of .iloc[0], or name the estimator in the evidence string.

title: Deaths on slip roads, service roads and 'other' road types on covered roads are in neither numerator
disclosure_where: methodology §5.1 and the road_class.py docstring define the classes by road-type codes 1-6, so other codes are left out by construction. road_class_baseline.csv publishes 'other interurban' deaths. The road-types page gives no count of covered-owner deaths that are left out.
factual_core: Interurban crashes on owners 1-3 coded as service road (7), slip road (8), local track (10) or 'Otro' (14) are in neither class's numerator. Since 2021 the Basque records code about 450 crashes a year as 'Otro', most of them on numbered roads.
materiality: The ratio moves by at most about 0.07 (3.40-3.47 in 2023 against 3.45), and the range stays within roughly 2.97-3.73. '3 to 4' is unchanged.
suggested_fix: Publish the covered-owner deaths left out, by road type and year, and assign 'Otro' crashes on numbered roads to a class by road name where possible.

title: The heading's 'deaths per kilometre of motorways' reverses if read as per kilometre of road
disclosure_where: The body sentence directly under the heading gives the unit: 'deaths per billion vehicle-kilometres'. The previous section's heading and text set 'per measured kilometre' as kilometres driven. The table-of-contents entry carries no unit.
factual_core: The heading and its table-of-contents entry say 'deaths per kilometre of motorways' without 'vehicle'. Per kilometre of road length, motorways have about 3.8 times the deaths of conventional roads, the reverse direction.
materiality: No number changes. A reader who sees only the heading or the table of contents could take it as per kilometre of road and get the direction reversed. The first body sentence corrects that.
suggested_fix: Write 'deaths per vehicle-kilometre' or 'deaths per kilometre driven' in the heading, which also fixes the table-of-contents entry.

title: The interval treats as exact kilometres the yearbook says were partly estimated in 2023, and ignores deaths clustered in the same crash
disclosure_where: data.html, long-run notes: 'The interval of the ratio of deaths per kilometre allows for Poisson error in the two death counts and takes the kilometres as exact'. data.html, interurban notes: 'The latest year, 2023, is partly estimated'. The long-run page links to these through its Method link, but nothing appears next to the claim. Clustering and the non-receipt of Catalan and Cantabrian data are not mentioned anywhere.
factual_core: The published 95% interval (3.03-3.92) uses only Poisson error in the two death counts and treats kilometres as exact (long_run.py:262-265). That ignores crashes with several deaths and any error in the denominators. Yearbook table 1.2.15 says Catalonia's and Cantabria's 2023 regional traffic was not received and was estimated by a growth rate. Six regions were expanded from partial counts.
materiality: The interval widens from 3.03-3.92 to about 3.00-3.97 with clustering, or about 2.9-4.1 under the more generous alternatives. The point estimate 3.45 and '3 to 4 times' are unchanged; that wording comes from the range of annual point estimates, not from the interval. The 2022 minimum of the range (3.04) is sensitive to the yearbook's type split; without it the range is 3.14-3.84, still '3 to 4'. Calling 2023 'networks whose traffic is measured' is loose for the 7% of traffic that was extrapolated.
suggested_fix: Next to the claim, add that the interval takes the kilometres as exact and that 2023 regional traffic is partly estimated (Catalonia's and Cantabria's extrapolated from 2022). Optionally widen the interval for multi-death crashes (sum of squared deaths), or give the pooled 2016-2023 ratio 3.39 (3.23-3.55) beside it.

title: Calculator gives unwarned estimates for combinations of inputs barely or never recorded together
disclosure_where: The warning texts state exactly what they count ('share this zone, crash type, road users and number involved'; 'on this road ... have this ...'). docs/research/SEVERITY_CALCULATOR.md lists the warnings. It also says 'For rare combinations (fewer than 20 similar recorded crashes) it extrapolates from its additive structure, and the page warns', and that unusual place combinations carry the rare-level warning. Nothing says that other joint combinations, or road × province, are unchecked. An unwarned estimate carries no caveat.
factual_core: The engine's check() warns only in these cases: - fewer than 20 training crashes in the zone × crash type × road-user set × number-involved cell; - fewer than 20 crashes on the chosen road for any single input level or road user; - two rare-type rules. It never checks joint combinations of the other inputs, or road × province. Stacked inputs can therefore give an unwarned estimate that rests on few or no jointly recorded crashes.
materiality: A small share of estimates is affected: about 0.3% of all form estimates under the attacker's definition, and about 0 when road users are counted individually. These rest on combinations essentially absent from the records. Their intervals are about twice as wide, which conveys much of the extra uncertainty. No published number changes. The cost is a missing caveat on some stacked scenarios, such as the 52.8% example and motorways in Lleida.
suggested_fix: Add a joint-support check (training crashes matching the road plus any two other inputs, or a nearest-neighbour count) and a road × province support check to the warnings. Alternatively, add one sentence to the notes saying that the warnings test single inputs and the similar-crash cell only.

title: Through-town 'average instead of the model' rule rests on a difference within noise that the 2016–2023 record reverses
disclosure_where: The calculator's rule text names 2022–2023 and the fit years (severity_model.py:1190). SEVERITY_CALCULATOR.md gives 0.4006 against 0.4043 on the 198 crashes. validation.html says the rule picked the average in three of eight test years, and that the test scores whichever was chosen (ROC-AUC 0.55). ML_MODEL_REVIEW.md:129-131 and SEVERITY_CALCULATOR.md:206-208 say that the average then predicted worse than the model would have (0.54 against 0.60). None of this is on the calculator page. The noise in the 2022–23 comparison is not quantified anywhere.
factual_core: The calculator shows the provincial average instead of an estimate on roads through towns. The rule rests on 2022–2023 validation, where the average beat the model by 0.0037 log loss per crash on 198 crashes (26 fatal). That difference is within noise. The same rule chose the model in 2017–2021, and over the 2016–2023 rolling test the model predicted through-town crashes slightly better than the average.
materiality: No number is wrong. Through-town scenarios show the observed provincial share with its count and Wilson interval (for example Lleida, 16 of 103, 9.8–23.8%). Only the justification is overstated: 'predicted later crashes better' should read 'predicted them about as well (0.401 against 0.404 on 198 crashes, a difference within noise)'. The rolling record favours the model only weakly, with a CI that includes 0, so the attacker's 'reverses' is not robust either. Neither predictor ranks these crashes well. The issue affects the 5% of crashes on roads through towns.
suggested_fix: Reword the rule text. For example: 'On 2022–2023 the average fatal share of such roads in the province predicted these crashes about as well as the model (log loss 0.401 against 0.404, 198 crashes), and the model barely ranks them, so the average is shown.' Alternatively, require a material margin before switching to the average.

title: The 2013–2024 plateau contains a 6% step in 2016 in the 30-day count, coinciding with the end of the 30-day/24-hour ratio dip; the plateau is not reconciled across series
disclosure_where: The yearly counts showing the step are in long-run.html Table 1, beside the claim. The 2011-2015 ratio dip ('a temporary dip, not a lasting step') is described in data.html (technical notes, 'Recording behind the long-run series', and the assumptions table) and in methodology sections 5 and 12, away from the claim. The long-run Limitations box says only that the 24-hour refit turns in the same years. No page discusses the 2016 step, its urban concentration or the 24-hour 2013-2024 comparison; the 24-hour plateau slope is only in longrun_projection_sensitivity.csv.
factual_core: In the 30-day count, every non-pandemic year from 2016 (1,746-1,830) exceeds every year of 2013-2015 (1,680-1,689): a level step of about +6.3%. The step is concentrated in urban deaths and coincides with the end of the disclosed 2011-2015 dip in the 30-day/24-hour ratio. In 24-hour deaths the step is about +3.5% and not clear. The site does not reconcile the plateau across the two series, and the headline's reference year 2013 sits in the dip.
materiality: The headline's direction is unchanged. In 24-hour deaths, counted directly by the police, 2013 to 2024 is +2.2%, the 2013-2019 slope is +0.64% a year (-0.7% to +2.0%), and the step is not clear (p 0.20-0.37). In 30-day deaths, a post-hoc step model makes the +6.3% clear at dispersion up to 1.45 (p 0.0015-0.013), but not at dispersion 3 (p 0.14), nor beyond the linear trend at 1.45 (p 0.068). About 2.7 of the 6.3 points coincide with the end of the ratio dip the site already attributes to the 2011 change of method. At the 2016-2024 mean ratio (about 1.164), 2013 would be about 1,733 and the 2013-2024 change about +3%. The sentence needs a qualifier (the 2016 step and the 24-hour comparison), not a reversal.
suggested_fix: Beside the headline, give the 24-hour comparison: 1,489 in 2013 and 1,522 in 2024, with a 2013-2019 slope of +0.6% a year (interval -0.7% to +2.0%). Add one sentence: the 30-day count stepped up about 6% in 2016, mostly in urban deaths, as the 30-day/24-hour ratio left its 2011-2015 dip, so the 2013 base sits in the dip.

title: 'No clear rise' since 2013 rests on a test with about 2% real size and about 40% power; correctly sized tests find a significant 2013–2019 rise in the 30-day count
disclosure_where: long-run.html prints '(95% interval -0.2% to +2.7%)' beside 'neither the count ... has a clear trend'. docs/methodology.md section 5 (linked from data.html) says 'a slight rise since 2013 cannot be ruled out' and explains the floor and the t quantile. The data.html notes say the deaths dispersion rests on seven years (interval 0.6-8.7). index.html gives no interval, only the counts 1,680 and 1,785. No page states the low power or the significance under Poisson or the normal quantile; the normal-quantile slope interval appears only in longrun_projection_sensitivity.csv.
factual_core: The printed 2013-2019 count slope (+1.2% a year, 95% interval -0.2% to +2.7%) is a quasi-Poisson fit with the Pearson scale floored at 1 and a t(5) quantile. The issue claims this procedure is conservative (real size about 0.7-2.8%), has about 40% power for +1.24% a year, and that correctly sized tests (Poisson, NB2, quasi-Poisson with the normal quantile, the calibrated statistic) reject 'no trend', so 'no clear rise or fall' overstates a borderline null.
materiality: No published number changes. The estimated dispersion (1.45) is above the floor, so the printed interval and p=0.074 are exactly those of the unfloored quasi-Poisson t(5) test, which is correctly sized at every true dispersion. Significance at 5% requires treating the dispersion as known and at most about 2: Poisson p=0.0066, calibrated p 0.018-0.049. The data do not establish that (dispersion interval 0.57-8.72). At most the wording changes: the symmetric 'no clear rise or fall' could become 'no fall, and a slight rise (about +1.2% a year to 2019, p about 0.07) that is not statistically clear', with the interval also on index.html. This is an imprecise wording, not an error.
suggested_fix: On index.html and in the long-run summary, word it asymmetrically: 'no fall since 2013, and a rise of about 1% a year to 2019 that is not statistically clear (95% interval -0.2% to +2.7%)'. Add that seven years give about 40% power to detect a rise of that size. Keep Student's t: the normal quantile is over-sized at the plausible dispersions, and dropping the floor changes nothing in this sample.

title: The 2020–2024 ranges over-cover (about 98–99% at the estimated dispersion) and continue a slope the page calls unclear
disclosure_where: long-run.html: Table 1 caption ('The trend continues the count's 2013-2019 trend') and the range definition in the paragraph above it. Methodology section 5 explains the floor and the t quantile. The data.html technical notes' Table 2 gives the normal-quantile and joinpoint-continued readings (count 2021: -18% below, -16% within); the CSV gives every year. trends.html gives 2024 against 2019 directly. No flat-plateau reading is shown.
factual_core: The 2020-2024 projection ranges of the count (2013-2019 segment refitted, quasi-Poisson with the scale floored at 1, t(5)) are claimed to cover about 98% of future years if the true dispersion is 1.45 (about 99% at 1), making 'within its range' lenient. They also extrapolate a +1.2% a year slope the page calls unclear, which produces the -7%, -5% and -8% 'against the trend' figures for 2022-2024; against the flat 2013-2019 mean these would be -0.3%, +3.1% and +1.9%.
materiality: No verdict changes: below in 2020-2021 and within from 2022 under the t5, normal-quantile, joinpoint-continued, 24-hour and flat-mean projections. Only a pure-Poisson normal interval moves 2022 below, by 3.5 deaths. The printed ranges are the unfloored t(5) intervals, with 95% coverage at any dispersion, so the over-coverage does not apply to them. Against a flat plateau, the 2022-2024 'Against the trend' figures would read -0.3%, +3.1% and +1.9% instead of -7%, -5% and -8%: a presentational difference.
suggested_fix: Add a flat-plateau reading (the 2013-2019 mean, 1,751) beside the rising trend, in Table 1 or the technical notes, or note that the -7% to -8% shortfalls of 2022-2024 come mostly from the extrapolated slope. Keep the t(5) ranges.

title: Turning points are chosen on the same data and segment intervals treat them as known; the plateau's slope depends on its start year
disclosure_where: In the data.html technical notes, directly above the segment table that prints the interval: 'The intervals in the table take the turning points as known.' Methodology section 5 reports the three-break QBIC (96.3 against 97.2) and the simplicity rule. long-run.html prints only the point estimate (10.9% a year). The start-year dependence of the count's plateau appears only in the start_2011 rows of longrun_projection_sensitivity.csv.
factual_core: The 2003 and 2013 turning points come from an exhaustive search on the same 1993-2019 data, and the segment intervals condition on them. With break uncertainty, the 2003-2013 interval widens from about -11.6% to -10.3% to about -12.1% to -10.0%. 2013 is chosen in about two thirds of bootstrap replicates. The plateau slope depends on its start year, and a three-break model has the lower QBIC.
materiality: No headline changes. '10.9% a year from 2003 to 2013' is robust: endpoint -11.0%, bootstrap median -10.96%, 24-hour deaths -10.8%. The technical-notes interval (-11.6% to -10.3%) would widen to about -12.2% to -10.0% with break uncertainty, about 75% wider. Plateau slopes for start years 2011-2014 range from -1.0% to +1.2% a year, none significant, and the bootstrap last-segment slope includes zero, so 'no clear rise or fall' holds under break uncertainty.
suggested_fix: In the technical notes, report bootstrap intervals for the segment slopes that re-run the turning-point search (2003-2013: about -12.2% to -10.0%), and the share of replicates that choose 2013 (about two thirds to 85%).

title: The "measured" 2023 interurban kilometres are partly estimated, and the 1.4-point drift depends on that year
disclosure_where: data.html long-run-interurban: 'The latest year, 2023, is partly estimated: the yearbook keeps the regional and provincial networks' lengths of the year before and takes the State network's traffic as the reference for all networks.' The trends explorer tool also says 'the latest year is partly estimated in the source'. long-run.html calls them measured, and methodology.md is silent.
factual_core: long-run.html calls the 2023 interurban vehicle-km 'measured' and builds the 1.4-point faster drift in km per tonne on them. The yearbook's 2023 figures for the regional and provincial networks use 2022 network lengths, and footnote (4) names the State network's traffic as the reference for all networks. Ending the drift in 2022 gives only 0.92 points over the 2011-2019 baseline.
materiality: The per-km reading (+5% against ±12%) does not move with a 1-2% error in the kilometres. The reconciliation sentence ('1.4 points... would fall within its range') has a margin of only 0.17 points a year. The attacker's comparison of 0.92 with 1.23 mixes a three-year drift to 2022 with a four-year requirement for 2023, so it does not show the reconciliation fails. The faster drift after 2019 already shows by 2022, and a 2013 base makes it larger rather than smaller.
suggested_fix: On long-run.html say that the 2023 kilometres are partly estimated, as the technical notes do, and give the 2019-2022 drift (0.9 points) beside the 2019-2023 drift.

title: 'Within' for admissions per resident and per vehicle depends on comparing with a flat 2019, not the falling pre-pandemic trend
disclosure_where: trends.html frames every claim as '2024 against 2019' (title, summary, Table 1 caption). Below Figure 1 it gives the trend reading for deaths per tonne only: 'Set against the falling trend of 2011–2019 instead of against 2019 ... 16% and 14% above ... or 10% and 8% for a trend started in 2013'. long-run.html says 'the two readings differ because the trend kept falling after 2019'. data.html (long-run notes) says 'the trend asks whether the decline of 2011–2019 went on, the comparison with 2019 whether the rate rose'. docs/methodology.md:203 says 'the statement on the Since 2019 page is about 2024 against 2019'. Nothing on the site gives a trend reading for admissions.
factual_core: The 2019-to-2024 intervals measure each count's scatter around its 2013–2019 trend but use the 2019 level as the reference. Admissions fell about 2% a year over 2013–2019. Against that trend projected to 2024, admissions are beyond its prediction interval under four of five denominators, so 'per resident, per licence holder and per registered vehicle the rise stays within it' holds only against 2019.
materiality: No published number or sentence is false: each statement is about the change since 2019, and against 2019 the admissions rows are within under three of five denominators (count -0.2% lower bound, per resident -3.7%, per licence holder -2.7%, per vehicle -5.8%). What readers are not told is that admissions had been falling about 2% a year and that 2024 is about 16–40% above the continued 2013–2019 path, beyond its range under four of five denominators. That would turn the per-tonne excess, which the page calls one that 'would vanish' with a 0.3%-a-year drift, into a robust one (+25% to +57%). But this verdict depends on the trend window for the count and per resident.
suggested_fix: Below the admissions paragraph, add one sentence, as the page already does for deaths per tonne. For example: 'Against the 2013–2019 trend, which fell about 2% a year, admissions in 2024 were about 20% above the projection (5% to 39%); the comparison with 2019 asks whether the level rose, the trend whether the decline went on.' Optionally add 'against 2019' to the admissions heading.

title: The admissions rise is urban, where provincial series show local-police recording ramping up after 2019
disclosure_where: trends.html section 2 names 'more complete tracing of admissions back to crashes' as a candidate cause and says a step in recorded urban crashes widens the crash intervals. Methodology section 4 and data.html describe only the 2013-2016 urban step. Post-2019 provincial ramps are not mentioned.
factual_core: 75% of the 2019-2024 admissions rise is on urban roads (4,310 to 5,025, against 4,303 to 4,536 interurban). The urban injury-crash counts of several provinces kept rising steeply after 2019 (14 provinces, 8,892 to 14,395) while the national urban count was flat. The attacker infers that more complete urban recording may partly drive the per-tonne 'beyond'.
materiality: There is no demonstrated effect on the admissions verdict beyond its knife-edge. The pre-2019-selected removals lower the per-tonne point estimate by 0.8-2.4 points, no more than random province removals of the same size. The post-2019-selected comparison (+37.5% against +11.7%) selects on a correlate of the outcome. For crashes, the ramps would make the 2019-2024 fall larger, which leaves 'crashes down, admissions per crash up' intact; the page already declines to judge the crash falls.
suggested_fix: In the crash paragraph, note that several provinces' recorded urban crashes kept rising after 2019 (e.g. Murcia, Cantabria, Salamanca), so the national change mixes recording coverage. Optionally show interurban admissions (+5.4%) beside the national figure.

title: February's 'interval below 1' is marginal: it fails family-wise correction over 12 months, the removal of one year, and half the alternative windows
disclosure_where: The page and the data page say only '95% intervals' and name the pooled years (2014-2024 without 2020-21; data.html#seasons-months, Figure 1 caption). Nothing on the pages, in docs/methodology.md or in the site source says that the twelve intervals are unadjusted for comparing 12 months, shows window sensitivity, or explains the 2014 start.
factual_core: February's per-tonne-of-fuel 95% interval (0.866-0.986) excludes 1 only per comparison. It fails family-wise control over the 12 months, touches 1 when 2014 or 2023 is dropped, and includes 1 in 5 of the attacker's 10 alternative windows. The 2014 start of PROFILE_YEARS is never justified.
materiality: With family-wise control (Holm or simultaneous intervals), the heading 'February to May below it' would lose February: adjusted p is 0.10-0.20 and the simultaneous interval is 0.838-1.019. Single-step simultaneous intervals would also put March and August at about 1. Under FDR control (BH q=0.03) nothing changes. The printed estimates (Feb 0.92; Feb-May 0.90-0.92) are unaffected. The claimed window dependence comes from lost power, not a changed estimate: longer windows, including the attacker's preferred one, keep February below 1.
suggested_fix: In the paragraph after Figure 1 (or the Figure 1 caption), add: 'The intervals are for each month separately; allowing for twelve comparisons, February's interval (the closest to 1) would include 1.' Alternatively, note in data.html#seasons-months that pooling from 2011 gives the same pattern, and say why the window starts in 2014.

title: 'The only monthly measure of traffic on all roads': CORES records sales whose timing moves with prices and taxes
disclosure_where: The phrase itself says 'road fuel sold', and section 2 of the seasons page says 'road fuel sold stands in for' kilometres. docs/methodology.md lines 368-370 say 'fuel sold, not kilometres driven ... a proxy rate', and trends.html#road-fuel mentions 'fuel bought in Spain but burnt elsewhere'. Sales timing around price and tax changes is mentioned nowhere. The page also calls petrol sold and toll traffic 'measures of traffic', so in its vocabulary 'measure' means indicator.
factual_core: CORES monthly 'consumo' is built from operators' declarations of sales, so monthly fuel sold moves with purchase timing around price and tax changes (the 2022 discount, the September 2012 VAT rise). The lead calls fuel sold 'the only monthly measure of traffic on all roads'. The effect on the pooled month effects is small.
materiality: No published number changes; pooled per-tonne effects move by at most about 0.02 when the year with the largest timing shocks is dropped, and the pattern is unchanged. Only the wording of the lead is affected.
suggested_fix: Reword the lead to 'Per tonne of road fuel sold, the only monthly series that covers all roads and a proxy for traffic, ...'. In the technical notes, add one sentence: monthly sales shift with purchase timing around price and tax changes (September 2012, April and December 2022), which adds noise to single months but not to the pooled pattern.

title: The April 2020 per-tonne fall reflects freight's larger share of the fuel still sold; per light-vehicle measures, deaths per unit rose
disclosure_where: The consequence is printed next to the claim. The section heading reads 'deaths fell more than road fuel sold and less than petrol or motorway traffic', and the same sentence gives petrol -76% and toll -78% beside deaths -68%. The page never reads the -24% as lower risk per km. The mechanism appears only elsewhere: docs/methodology.md lines 369-370 ('mixes freight with private travel') and trends.html#road-fuel ('the mix of freight and private travel ... a change per tonne cannot be read as a change per kilometre'), which is linked from section 2 of the seasons page, not from the lockdown section. Nothing tells the reader why fuel fell less than light traffic.
factual_core: In April 2020 freight kept running while light traffic collapsed. Diesel fell less than petrol, and heavy toll traffic far less than light toll traffic, so road fuel fell less than light-vehicle traffic. Deaths therefore fell per tonne of fuel but rose per tonne of petrol and per toll vehicle. Under assumed freight shares of fuel, the change per vehicle-km is on both sides of zero.
materiality: No published number or ordering changes. What is missing is one explanatory clause: freight (diesel -54%, heavy toll -29%) held up while light traffic collapsed (petrol -76%, light toll -86%), so per tonne understates the per-km change in the lockdown. The page already shows that per-unit deaths rose against the light-traffic measures (deaths fell less than petrol and toll). The modelled per-km change of -19% to +18% rests on unverified assumptions.
suggested_fix: After the -24%, add: 'Diesel, which carries most freight, fell 54% and heavy toll traffic 29%, against 76% for petrol and 86% for light toll traffic, so the fuel still sold stood for fewer kilometres than before and the fall per tonne overstates any fall per kilometre.'

title: The falsification tests use the straight-line trend the page rejects; with the better-fitting pre-trend family, July 2006 has the largest step of any July and a calibrated step interval excluding zero
disclosure_where: site/policy.html, placebo paragraph: 'Fitted with a straight-line trend at July 2006 and at every other July ...'. site/data.html: 'The same step model, with a straight-line trend ...'. methodology §14 attributes the too-narrow intervals to 'a straight or once-bent trend'. No page reports the placebos under the chosen bend or under level-shift pre-trends.
factual_core: The calendar placebos, the placebo-calibrated interval and the forecast test use a straight-line pre-trend (policy.py:560-600, 697-724), while the main fit uses the QAIC-chosen bend. Rerun with the pre-trend chosen by QAIC in each window, July 2006 ranks behind July 2004 within the bend family. Within a family that also allows a level shift, it has the clearly largest step and a calibrated step interval that excludes zero.
materiality: Within the page's own preferred family (straight plus bend), nothing changes. With the bend chosen in each window, July 2006 falls to 2nd on the step, 8th-10th on the 17-month average and 10th on the forecast. The calibrated interval still includes zero. So the straight-line choice is, if anything, conservative for the page's claim. Only under the level-shift family (issue 1's premise) does the step stand out (-12.3% vs -7.2%) with a calibrated interval excluding zero. Even there, the 17-month average (-11.3% vs -9.7%; -11.5% vs -11.2%) and the forecast (-11.4% vs -10.0%) remain 'nearly as large', and the calibrated 17-month interval includes zero. The 'close to nominal' claim relies on switching to quasi-Poisson errors. With the page's Newey-West errors, 3/14 and 4/12 placebo intervals still exclude zero, against 0.7 and 0.6 expected, so 'the model's intervals are too narrow' stands.
suggested_fix: Add the placebos and forecasts with the pre-trend chosen in each window. If issue 1's fix is adopted, report July 2006's rank under each pre-trend family: second within bends, first by a clear margin on the step but narrowly on the 17-month average under level shifts. Keep the Newey-West counts of placebo intervals that exclude zero.

title: CORES fuel enters with a negative coefficient, so 'barely moves the step' says nothing about exposure
disclosure_where: site/policy.html, next to the claim: 'but neither series measures kilometres on all roads'. site/data.html repeats the step sentence. docs/methodology.md §14: 'Neither moves the estimate materially: the step does not track these traffic measures, and neither measures exposure.' The coefficient and its sign are reported nowhere.
factual_core: In the published fuel-covariate fit, the centred log of CORES road-fuel tonnes has a negative coefficient: -0.50 (HAC se 0.20) under the chosen bend and -0.29 under the straight line. So more fuel goes with fewer deaths. Toll-motorway intensity enters at +0.37 (se 0.16). The page reports only that the step barely moves.
materiality: No published number changes, and 'barely moves the step' is true. Because fuel enters with the wrong sign for exposure under every pre-trend tried, the fuel fit does not show that traffic leaves the step unexplained. The page and methodology already hedge ('neither measures exposure'), so the gap is that the coefficients are unreported.
suggested_fix: Report both covariate coefficients in the sensitivity table. Say that fuel enters with a negative sign, so the fuel fit is not an exposure check, and that toll intensity enters positively but covers a small part of the network.

title: '6 of the 14 other Julys ... where about 0.7 would be expected' mostly reflects the Newey–West estimator, not a wandering trend
disclosure_where: The estimator's small-sample bias is not disclosed. The causal diagnosis being questioned ('most likely because a straight or once-bent trend does not capture how the series wanders') appears only in docs/methodology.md section 14. policy.html and data.html give the 6-of-14 count and the 2.5x ratio without a cause.
factual_core: If each of the 14 placebo windows were generated by its own correct no-effect straight-line model with NB noise, the NW12 step interval would exclude zero about 30% of the time, about 4.4 of 14. Refitted with quasi-Poisson or NB2-ML errors, 2 of 14 placebo steps exclude zero and the z spread is about 1.4. On this account, the published 6-of-14 count and the 2.5x ratio mostly reflect the estimator, and the methodology's 'trend wanders' diagnosis is largely wrong.
materiality: No published number changes. The page sentences ('6 of the 14 ... where about 0.7 would be expected'; 'vary 2.5 times as much as the model's standard errors imply') are literally correct about the NW12 model, and 'intervals too narrow' is right. With valid errors they would read 2 of 14 and about 1.4 times. The calibrated interval (-21% to +3%) uses the empirical placebo spread and is unaffected. The page's attribution argument rests on step ranks and the 2003 bend, not on this calibration. What is wrong is the methodology's attribution for the step: about 2.0 of the 2.46 ratio is estimator bias.
suggested_fix: In methodology section 14, say that under a correct model the NW12 interval would exclude zero at about 4.4 of the 14 placebos, and report the count under quasi-Poisson errors (2 of 14). Keep the trend-wander explanation for the 17-month average and the slope change, where it survives valid errors.

title: Under the preferred bend, the 'immediate fall' is a July–August 2006 dip; the year-long wearing away comes from the linear slope term
disclosure_where: site/policy.html says 'fitted deaths rejoin the projected path in about July 2007', which marks the statement as model-based. Figure 1's lower panel ('enlarged from January 2005') plots the observed monthly deaths with the fit and both projections, so the summer dip is visible. The text never describes the monthly pattern or the July-August concentration.
factual_core: Against the bend projection fitted to the pre-period only, July-August 2006 are 13.8% below and September 2006-November 2007 0.9% below. A break at September 2006 gives a step of +0.7%. So the 'immediate fall of about 7%' followed by a twelve-month linear return is the shape the step-plus-slope model imposes, not the monthly pattern.
materiality: No published number changes; the 17-month average of -2.5% uses the same data. The description would change from 'fell 7% and returned over about a year' to 'fell about 14% in July-August 2006; about 4% below the projection through February 2007 and near it afterwards'. A linear return is one parametric summary; the data fit a two-month dip at least as well. This is a wording point.
suggested_fix: Add one sentence describing the monthly pattern: deaths were about 14% below the projection in July-August 2006, about 4% below through February 2007, and near it afterwards. Say that the gradual return to July 2007 is the shape of the fitted model.

title: Unknown-age drivers are disproportionately hit-and-run, so 'their ages follow the recorded mix' is doubtful (effect upward, small)
disclosure_where: data.html section 'Drivers whose age is not recorded' states the assumption and the 2.96 bound; the drivers page Limitations says 2.3% are left out. The hit-and-run composition is not mentioned.
factual_core: Many drivers of unrecorded age fled the scene: 27% of them in DGT tables 4.4, against 0.1-0.2% of drivers of known age. So the assumption that their ages follow the recorded mix may fail, probably towards younger drivers, which would raise the 18-29 ratio slightly (bounded at 2.96).
materiality: The plausible effect is +0.4% to +1% (2.68 to about 2.69-2.70). The disclosed bound is +10.5% (2.96). It works against the transfer bias, and the conclusion does not change.
suggested_fix: Beside the limitation, add that many drivers of unknown age fled the scene, so if they are younger than average the 18-29 ratio would be slightly higher (at most 2.96).

title: The drivers page states the condition only as 'rests on Madrid's survey alone', and says no Barcelona-area survey separates 75+
disclosure_where: The drivers-page sentence names Madrid's survey, gives the full range and says the data do not establish a difference. The figure caption says 65–74 and 75+ use the Madrid split. The full condition ('If people aged 75 and over in Spain in 2024 drive as much less as in Madrid...') and the 65+ grouping and 2016 strata are on the methodology page, linked as 'why' from the sentence. The routing ratio is only in DRIVER_AGE_EXPOSURE.md.
factual_core: Commit 268caf2 replaced the drivers page's explicit condition ('If people aged 75 and over drive as much less than those aged 65–74 as in Madrid in 2018 ... a conditional estimate that holds only on that assumption') with 'no survey of the Barcelona area separates their driving from that of people aged 65–74, so it rests on Madrid's survey alone'. The attacker says this no longer states the place-and-time transfer, that the 'no survey' clause is inaccurate (EMEF strata until 2016, P1b routing), and that the EMEF routing ratio (0.25–0.27 against 0.30) points higher.
materiality: No number changes. The sentence would gain the explicit if-clause, and 'no survey ... separates' would become 'the Barcelona-area survey's public files group everyone aged 65 and over'. The routing ratio's interval contains Madrid's 0.30 and comes from 2014-2016, so citing it would not move 2.43 or the conclusion.
suggested_fix: Restore 'if people aged 75 and over in Spain drive as much less than those aged 65–74 as in Madrid in 2018' in the 75+ sentence. Say 'the Barcelona-area survey's public files group everyone aged 65 and over' and that the split at 75 rests on Madrid's survey. Extend the guard test to require the condition clause.

title: The central 75+ figure moved from 2.06 to 2.43 by a post-hoc choice of profile in the final commit; audits and range analysis not updated

It prints the Barcelona-only 2.06 (1.6–2.6) next to 2.43, and the Table 13 caption and the range text say the one-at-a-time analysis starts from the Barcelona profile with Madrid's split (2.06). docs/methodology.md:444-450 and the DRIVER_AGE_EXPOSURE.md header say the same. Add a one-line change note on the methodology page that the central moved from the Barcelona profile (2.06) to the average (2.43) in October 2026.

title: 'In every age band' rests on a 65–74 lower bound of 1.03 and on the chosen three-year window
disclosure_where: The sentence says 'pooling 2022-2024' and Figure 3's title gives 2022-2024. Figure 3, directly under the claim, plots the 65-74 interval nearly touching 1, and drivers_sex_ratios.csv gives low = 1.0317. The page does not say that other windows lose significance in one band.
factual_core: For 2022-2024 every band's men/women deaths-per-involved interval excludes 1, but 65-74 only narrowly (1.55, 1.03-2.33). In neighbouring three-year windows at least one band's interval includes 1 (2021-2023 65-74: 1.36, 0.90-2.06; 2020-2022 75+: 1.59, 0.94-2.71). The band involvement-per-licence ratios also vary from year to year more than Poisson error allows.
materiality: No published number or sentence changes: 'in every age band' is true for the stated 2022-2024 window under Poisson, binomial and exact intervals. Read as 'significantly higher in every band', it would fail in 7 of 9 three-year windows. Read as 'higher in every band', which is the wording and the figure alt text ('Men's rates are above women's ... in every age band'), it holds in every window. The extra-Poisson variation in involvement per licence would at most double interval widths that sit far above 1 (lowest band lower bound 1.36).
suggested_fix: Write 'in every age band (from 1.55 at 65-74, 95% interval 1.03-2.33, to 3.09 at 18-24)', or pool 2020-2024, where every band's interval excludes 1 (65-74: 1.73, 1.23-2.43).

title: The km split by sex comes from Spain's most metropolitan regions, and the surveys' own gradients point to men's share being overstated, biasing the ratio toward 'men safer per km'
disclosure_where: Next to the claim, drivers.html says 'a gap small enough that other assumptions about who drives how far could reverse it'. The range 0.60-1.23 appears in risk_sex_per_km.csv (linked from the page), in docs/methodology.md §7.1 and in docs/research/DRIVER_AGE_EXPOSURE.md. The research document is linked at the foot of the page and concludes that 'men are involved about as often as women'. data.html says the sampling intervals are probably too narrow because the survey samples in clusters. Nowhere is it said which way the less metropolitan and licence-calibrated profiles move the ratio, toward 1 or above it.
factual_core: The per-km sex ratio depends on men's share of car km, which is carried to Spain from the Barcelona-province and Madrid-region surveys. Within the EMEF, men's share falls as car dependence rises. Licence calibration and evidence from settlement patterns suggest Spain's share is below the central 66.6%. If so, the printed 0.91 (0.87-0.95) leans toward 'men involved less per km'. The page gives neither the profile range nor this direction.
materiality: Under the package's own licence-calibrated transfer applied to both surveys, the central estimate would be about 0.95 rather than 0.91, and 0.98 with age adjustment as well. Excluding the Barcelona core gives about 0.98-1.06 (attacker). The page's qualitative message survives: no established per-km difference in involvement, and men killed 2.6 times as often per km under every profile (1.75-3.55). So does 'comes from their driving further' in aggregate, since at a ratio of 0.95-1.0 almost all of the 1.39 per licence holder is distance. What changes is that the printed point estimate and its 0.87-0.95 interval, which excludes 1, probably lean the wrong way. 'Plausibly 0.95-1.05' and 'men higher' are not established: the Madrid-region profile gives 0.907, and Madrid city's ECEPOV share is typical.

title: The per-km sex range varies only the regional profile; the 49% of DGT car km the surveys do not cover gets the weekday metropolitan sex split
disclosure_where: drivers.html, next to the claim: 'a gap small enough that other assumptions about who drives how far could reverse it'. data.html says the sex split is 'carried to Spain in the same way as by age', and states the 51% working-day coverage for age. docs/methodology.md describes the range as covering the regional profiles.
factual_core: risk_sex_per_km's range_low and range_high (involvement 0.60-1.23, killed 1.75-3.55) are the minimum and maximum over the regional profiles only (A, A2, four EMEF sub-areas, Madrid 2018). They leave out the distance, survey-year, professional-driving, employment, weekend and coverage alternatives used for age. The roughly 49% of DGT car km outside the surveys' working days is given the working-day sex split.
materiality: No published number or sentence changes. The omitted single-choice alternatives fall inside the existing range, so adding them would not move it. The involvement sentence already says the gap could reverse. The killed ratio stays far above 1 under every alternative. Applied to the average profile, the EMEF alternatives would move the central involvement ratio by roughly 5% either way, which the adjacent hedge covers. The weekend and coverage scenarios for sex are not computed, and their direction is unknown.
suggested_fix: Describe the risk_sex_per_km range as 'across the regional profiles', and add one sentence that the kilometres outside the surveys' working days are given the same sex split. Optionally add the distance, year and professional variants, which leave the range unchanged.

title: The Poisson intervals ignore clustering of same-type vehicles within crashes and the error in DGT's kilometres
disclosure_where: The general data.html section says 'Rates carry 95% intervals that treat counts as Poisson with a known denominator'. The data.html vehicle notes (vehicles.py:316-317) say 'The intervals in the result tables reflect the crash counts only and treat the kilometres as exact'. docs/methodology.md section 15 says the same. Neither appears on the vehicles page next to 'its 95% interval is clear'. Clustering within crashes is not mentioned anywhere.
factual_core: The exact Poisson intervals in q6_rates_2022 treat each vehicle involvement as independent and the kilometres as exact. Same-type vehicles cluster within crashes, which inflates the variance, and the kilometres are model estimates.
materiality: No published sentence changes. On the Catalan proxy, the involvement intervals for cars, vans and light trucks are about 1.3-1.4 times too narrow, and heavy trucks' about 1.1-1.2 times. The ratios to cars printed on the page carry no interval at all, although section 15 says ratios carry log-normal intervals.
suggested_fix: Add a sentence to the vehicles page's limitation: 'The intervals cover chance in the crash counts only; they treat each vehicle as independent, although several vehicles of one type can be in the same crash, and they take DGT's kilometres as exact.' Optionally widen the intervals by the square root of sum(k^2)/sum(k), or use a crash-level bootstrap where per-crash counts exist.

title: 'About the same rate per kilometre' for heavy-truck occupants rests on overlapping intervals in one year and does not replicate
disclosure_where: The sentence itself prints '1.9 against 2.2 per billion km; the 95% intervals overlap'. docs/methodology.md section 8 lists the 2022 intervals, 1.43-2.53 against 2.08-2.42. The code's own check (site/vehicles.py:128-132) tests 'below cars', with overlapping intervals'. That the gap is significant when pooled is not stated anywhere.
factual_core: In 2022, heavy-truck occupant deaths per km (1.93) against cars' (2.25) give a ratio of 0.86 (95% 0.64-1.14). The page calls the two rates 'about the same'. In 2021, 2023 and 2024 the ratio is significantly below 1.
materiality: The 2022 ratio (0.86) is close to the nine-year pooled 0.81. 2022 is therefore representative, and 'does not replicate' overstates the case: the year-to-year differences are consistent with chance (p=0.32). The pooled ratio, though, is significantly below 1, about a fifth lower. 'About the same' therefore understates a real gap of about 20%; 'somewhat lower than cars' (1.9 against 2.2)' would be accurate. The contrast with 2.5 times the involvement, and the conclusion that a measure built from occupant deaths alone misses most deaths in heavy-truck crashes, are unaffected; a lower occupant rate strengthens them.
suggested_fix: Replace 'about the same rate per kilometre as cars' with 'a somewhat lower rate per kilometre than cars' (1.9 against 2.2 per billion km in 2022, a difference within chance that year; about a fifth lower over 2016-2024)'.

title: Outcome-dependent recording cannot be bounded; modest differentials would produce every interurban ratio
disclosure_where: speed.html, section 'The ratio describes police records, not measured speeds', directly below Table 1: 'Police may look harder for speed when someone has died, which would raise it ... The data cannot measure either bias.' The same page's lede says the ratios are 'associations in police records, not estimates of what speed causes'. The home page intro says each comparison is 'an association in the records, not an estimate of what caused it'. Methodology section 9 ends with the two biases; factors.py docstring. The size of the differential that would produce each ratio is not given anywhere.
factual_core: Suppose speed has no real effect, there are no false positives and deaths are rare. If police record speed k times as often in fatal crashes, the deaths-per-crash ratio comes out at about k. So the interurban ratios (1.22, 1.75, 1.90) need only a modest k, while the urban 5.90 needs about 5 to 6. Nothing in the repository can bound k.
materiality: No published number changes. Every sentence is about crashes 'in which the police recorded' speed and stays true. As evidence about speed, the interurban ratios are fragile: they would be fully produced if fatal crashes had speed recorded about 1.2-1.7 times as often as non-fatal ones. The urban ratio would need roughly five-fold differential recording. Its hospitalised-injury ratio (2.49) also points the same way, so the 'most of all on urban streets' ranking is robust.
suggested_fix: Add one sentence to the speed page's recording paragraph. With no real difference, recording speed k times as often after a death gives a ratio of about k. The interurban ratios (1.2-1.9) are within reach of such a differential; the urban 5.9 would need it about five-fold.

title: The 2.00 (1.69–2.36) summary depends on the pooling frame; random-effects intervals are far wider
disclosure_where: speed.html, next to the claim: 2.00 is called 'their weighted summary' after the 1.22-5.90 range, and the paragraph after Table 1 says it 'describes no single kind of road: it is weighted towards other interurban roads'. The data.html technical notes and methodology.md section 9 give LR 446 on 3 df, the fall in dispersion from 13.5 to 2.0, and 'a weighted summary, dominated by other interurban roads'. Not stated: that the interval holds only for that fixed weighting and would be several times wider for a typical road type. The home page gives 2.0 with the 1.2-5.9 range and no interval.
factual_core: The 2.00 (1.69-2.36) summary is the speed coefficient of a common-ratio quasi-Poisson model: 64 cells, 52 df, dispersion 13.48, z quantile. The data reject a common ratio (LR 446 on 3 df). Other standard summaries give 1.92-2.22. Random-effects intervals over the four road types are several times wider (DL 1.09-4.51, HKSJ 0.75-6.56, prediction interval 0.07-71). So the stated precision applies only to a fixed-set, death-weighted reading.
materiality: No published number changes. Under the reading the page states (a weighted summary of four road types that partition all crashes), the published interval is conservative: fixed-set intervals are narrower (fixed effect 1.97-2.24; year bootstrap 1.80-2.20; published 1.69-2.36). Only under a random-effects 'typical road type' reading, which the page disclaims, is it 4.2 times (DL) to 6.5 times (HKSJ) too narrow in log width. The point value is robust at about 2 (1.92-2.22). What remains is wording: 'its interval is widened to allow for how much the ratios differ', and the home page's 2.0 without the weighting named.
suggested_fix: Replace 'its interval is widened to allow for how much the ratios differ' (and the Figure 1 caption's 'also for the differences between road types') with a statement of scope: e.g. 'its interval applies to this weighting of the four road types; it is not a range for any one road type, whose ratios run from 1.22 to 5.90'. Optionally note in the technical notes that an unweighted (random-effects) mean over the four types is about 2.2 with an interval of about 1.1-4.5.

title: Part of the urban and interurban excess is time-of-week composition
disclosure_where: speed.html lede: 'associations in police records, not estimates of what speed causes'. Below Table 1: the ratio does not 'separate speed from other factors recorded in the same crash'. Home page intro caveat. Time of day or week is not named on the speed page, in methodology section 9 or in the data-page speed notes.
factual_core: Crashes with speed recorded are concentrated at night and at weekends. Stratifying by zone, hour and weekday (2014-2023, Mantel-Haenszel) lowers the urban ratio from 5.59 to 4.84 and the interurban ratio from 1.66 to 1.56.
materiality: Applying the same relative change to the published 2016-2023 ratios gives about 5.1 for urban streets instead of 5.90. The interurban road-type ratios would be about 6% lower (about 1.15, 1.65 and 1.79). The ranking, the 'deadlier on every road type' description and 'most of all on urban streets' all stand.
suggested_fix: Optionally add a sensitivity sentence: adjusted for hour and day of week (2014-2023), the urban ratio falls by about an eighth (5.6 to 4.8) and the interurban by about 6%; the ranking is unchanged.

title: 'Urban streets' includes travesías (through-towns) and urban motorways
disclosure_where: data.html glossary: 'Zone: DGT's grouping of roads into interurban roads, and urban streets and crossings'. Methodology section 3: 'urban street and crossing'. The severity page explains 'urban crossing' as a conventional road through a town. Nothing on the speed page or home page. Urban motorways are not mentioned anywhere for the speed comparison. The crash explorer, linked from the speed page, uses 'Urban streets' for road code 9 only.
factual_core: The row labelled 'Urban streets' is the report's 'Vías urbanas', which the report defines as 'calles y travesías'. In the microdata the urban zone also includes urban motorways (ZONA 4). In scope for 2016-2023, travesías have 3,440 crashes and 195 deaths, and urban motorways 2,620 crashes and 20 deaths.
materiality: A label problem only. Travesías are 1.0% of urban crashes but 6.6% of urban deaths. Removing them would put the urban ratio at roughly 4.9-6.2 instead of 5.90 under plausible assumptions. No published number is wrong, and the ranking and the home-page finding are unchanged.
suggested_fix: Label the category 'urban roads (streets and through-town roads)' on the speed page and home page, or footnote Table 1 with DGT's definition.

title: On-duty variant understates the bias it is cited for: trip motive is unknown for most drivers
disclosure_where: data.html, the sentence right after Table 10, gives the direction: 'more likely biased down than up' and 'drivers recorded as on duty'. docs/research/DRIVER_AGE_EXPOSURE.md:365-371 says 'biased down by an unknown amount. Two variants of the numerator test part of this'. docs/methodology.md:578-581 says the same. That half the motives are unknown is disclosed nowhere.
factual_core: The on-duty variant removes only drivers whose motive is recorded as on duty. The motive is 'Es desconeix' or blank for 48.4/52.1/56.2/65.6/62.5% of working-day car drivers aged 16-29/30-44/45-64/65-74/75+. If unknown-motive drivers were on duty as often as recorded ones, the 65+ ratios would be 0.905/1.256/1.060, and the middle version's 95% interval would exclude 1.
materiality: Under plausible recording rates (r1 0.6-0.9), the 65+ middle ratio rises a further 0.01-0.05 beyond the published variant, and every interval still includes 1. Only the extreme equal-recording assumption gives 1.26 (1.02-1.54). Part of the published correction may even be too large, because 'En missio' errands are partly in the denominator. The 'neither confirms nor rules out' reading is unchanged.
suggested_fix: Next to the 0.85-1.17, add that the trip motive is unknown for about half the drivers (two-thirds at 65 and over), so the variant removes only part of the on-duty drivers. Also say that the EMEF does count ordinary respondents' work-errand trips.

title: Knock-ons: 2024 car-km level (drivers Tables 7–8) and V11/V19 reasoning
disclosure_where: data.html Table 7 note: 'its other kilometre totals change the rates (from 356 to 376 per billion km at 65 and over) but not the ratios'. The drivers.html limitations say DGT's totals are 'valid only in aggregate'. Table 8 already spans -3% to 29% unexplained. The estimation vintage is not mentioned.
factual_core: Two published elements depend on the vintage of the 2024 estimate: - the 2024 car-km level, 289.8 bn excluding taxis and ride-hailing cars (Table 8: working days 146.5 bn, 51%); - Table 7's absolute rates. If the 2024 0-4 cars kept their 2022 or 2023 band mean, car km would be 17.35 or 20.82 bn higher. The working-day share would then be 47.7% or 47.2%, and the rates 5.6-6.7% lower. Ratios would be unaffected.
materiality: The premise that the 2024 level is understated is unverified: DGT says its new method improved precision. Even if the premise holds, a level shift of about 6% sits within the level uncertainty already shown. The findings on the drivers page are ratios.
suggested_fix: Note in the Table 8 caption that the 2024 level comes from a re-methodised DGT estimate that may differ from earlier vintages by several per cent.

title: Unverified: crash type, vehicle age, seat-belt use and age-differential recording of slight-injury crashes cannot be tested with the age tables
disclosure_where: data.html (data.txt:78) says deaths per crash depend on how completely slight-injury crashes are recorded, and that this split is used on the Drivers page. The home page frames comparisons as associations. The drivers page says the rate does not show who caused a crash or the danger to others. Recording that differs by age, and the lack of adjustment for crash type or vehicle, are not mentioned.
factual_core: The 75+ against 45–64 comparison cannot be adjusted for crash type, road type within zone, vehicle age or belt use. Nor can it be checked for age-differential recording of slight-injury crashes. The reason is that DGT's tables cross driver age only with sex, zone, vehicle type and licence seniority, and the crash microdata carry no driver age. If slight-injury crashes at 75+ were under-recorded, the 75+ rate would be inflated.
materiality: The bias is unknown but bounded. Lowering the ratio to 2.0 would need about 42% of 75+ involvements, relative to 45–64, to be missing, and the proxies show no sign of age-differential selection. The likeliest mechanism, frailty turning older drivers' minor collisions into recorded injury crashes, would make 3.4 conservative. Crash type, vehicle age and belt use could explain the gap, but they are not errors in a descriptive statement that claims no cause.
suggested_fix: Optional: add a clause on the drivers page saying the comparison is crude (not adjusted for sex, road, crash type or vehicle) and counts only police-recorded injury crashes.

title: Moped kilometres are imputed to an old 'circulating' fleet; crash data fit over-imputation
disclosure_where: The page's limitation says 'The kilometres are DGT's modelled estimates for 2022, valid for aggregates rather than for individual vehicles'. data.html and docs/methodology.md section 8 name DGT's 'parque circulante' and say the kilometres are modelled. None of them defines 'circulating', mentions the 37% of vehicles that stay modelled, or gives the age profile of the moped fleet.
factual_core: DGT's circulating fleet includes old, possibly dormant mopeds, and 37% of vehicles keep modelled kilometres. Crash involvement per km falls steeply with moped age. The attacker reads this as over-imputation of kilometres, which would understate the moped rate per km.
materiality: In the intermediate scenario no sentence changes: mopeds stay second, their interval still overlaps buses', and motorcycles' lower bound of 39.5 stays clear of the moped upper bound of 35.6. Only the extreme scenario makes motorcycles' interval touch the mopeds' (40.5 against 39.5), affecting 'its 95% interval is clear of every other type's'. Motorcycles' rank and the per-vehicle ranking are unaffected in every scenario.
suggested_fix: Define the circulating fleet in the page's limitation: 'vehicles with any DGT record in the past ten years; DGT models the kilometres of those without an inspection reading'. Optionally note that 70% of circulating mopeds are 15 or more years old, and give the moped rate with the 15+ band's kilometres down-weighted as a sensitivity.

title: Barcelona road-user shares compare groups with different selection into the file
disclosure_where: In the same paragraph, the lead says the file holds 'every person involved' and that 'These are shares of people in recorded crashes, not rates per journey'. '(3 of 4,671, 0.06%)' shows the size of the car-driver group and its events. The Figure 1 caption says 'as a share of the people in recorded crashes with a recorded injury outcome'.
factual_core: Most car drivers in the Barcelona person file are uninjured (82.2%), against 9.7% of pedestrians and 11.9% of motorcycle drivers. As a result the pedestrian-to-car-driver contrast in the serious-or-fatal share (6.5% against 0.06%, about 100 times) shrinks to about 20 times among injured people only. The attacker calls this selection bias in the published comparison.
materiality: No published number or sentence changes. The page states no ratio, only 'far more often', and that still holds under the attacker's own alternative: 7.2% against 0.36%, with non-overlapping intervals (5.7–9.0% against 0.1–1.1%). The denominator is the stated quantity, serious injury among people involved in recorded crashes, which is the standard 'killed or seriously injured per person involved' measure. The car drivers' low share is the occupant protection being measured, not an artefact. Police attendance under-records damage-only car crashes, which would raise the car-driver share, not lower it.
suggested_fix: None required. Optionally add: 'Most car drivers in the records were unhurt; among injured people only, the shares are 7.2% for pedestrians and 0.4% for car drivers.'

title: 'At least one death per crash' mixes per-person lethality with how many people were involved
disclosure_where: severity.html, the paragraph after the lead: '1.6% had at least one death within 30 days. An odds ratio compares the odds of a death in crashes with a circumstance...'. Figure 1 is titled 'Odds of at least one death, by crash circumstance' and captioned 'Odds ratios for at least one death in an injury crash'. data.html: 'DGT's file has one row per injury crash, with counts of the people killed and injured, but no record of individual drivers, vehicles or people. ... one for at least one death within 30 days'.
factual_core: The outcome is at least one death per crash, so crash types involving more people have higher per-crash odds of a death at the same per-person risk. The attacker says the per-crash head-on contrast therefore partly reflects how many people were involved.
materiality: None. The published odds ratios are correct for the stated per-crash outcome. The model adjusts for the number of vehicles, and occupancy cannot be separated from crash violence with this file. The ranking 'pedestrian struck and head-on far above every other circumstance' holds on a per-victim basis too.
suggested_fix: None required. Optionally change the lead sentence's 'the odds of a death within 30 days' to 'the odds of at least one death within 30 days'.

title: December 2025 has the lowest serious share of any month in five years of files: possible incomplete follow-up (unconfirmed)
disclosure_where: Follow-up completeness is not discussed, but the evidence above shows no need for it. data.html (sources and licence paragraph) states the file vintage: '2025 files last modified on 17 February 2026'.
factual_core: In December 2025, 9 of 610 crashes (1.48%) were serious or fatal, against 3.41% in January-November. The attacker attributes this to incomplete follow-up of the last weeks before the files' 2026-02-17 modification date, and says earlier years show no such dip.
materiality: No effect is established, and the page makes no claim by month. Only if the dip were an artefact would the person headline move from 1.641% to 1.715% (printed 1.7%) and the crash share from 3.26% to 3.41%. The evidence does not support that premise.
suggested_fix: None required. Optionally, the frequency notes could say that December has had a below-average serious share in every year since 2016.

title: The 'shares by crash type, which the site gives instead' are not the table that was compared, and they rank crashes clearly worse than the model
disclosure_where: barcelona.html, in the same sentence as the claim (barcelona.txt:27): 'model and shares alike read the crash type as recorded, the code above included'. The paragraph just before it (barcelona.txt:26) says the code records the outcome, gives 26 of 43 against 2 of 1,672, and says the page counts both as rear-end collisions. The CSV linked from the page carries the as-recorded shares. Methodology section 20 (docs/methodology.md:1275-1281) states the descriptive tables merge the code while the source models used the field as recorded.
factual_core: The model was compared with the 17-code accident-type table as recorded, in which 'Encalç' is its own level (26 of 43 serious). Figure 3 on barcelona.html shows merged shares, with Encalç folded into rear-end collisions. On the test rows the merged shares rank at ROC-AUC 0.686, against 0.734 for the compared table and 0.737 for the model. The attacker concludes the page wrongly presents its shares as an equally good substitute, and that the model card wrongly says 'the table is what the site shows'.
materiality: None for the published claim. The comparison it reports (as-recorded model against as-recorded shares) is stated as such. With both merged, the model is still no better on the published test (-0.016). The 0.686 against 0.737 contrast mixes codings: it credits the model with an outcome-recording code that the page says should not be read as a crash type. The model card's 'the table is what the site shows' is accurate, since the as-recorded table is in the site's CSV.
suggested_fix: Optional clarity only: 'the shares by crash type as recorded (given in the table below), which the site gives instead'.

title: 'Lorry or bus' is asserted, but the source does not define the heavy-vehicle class; the project's own notes say buses may not be in it
disclosure_where: The site does not caveat the label. A caveat is unnecessary, because the label is correct.
factual_core: The site labels the class 'a lorry or bus', but the source does not define F_VEH_PESANTS_IMPLICADES, and the project's own harmonisation note says buses may not be in it. The attacker concludes that whether buses are included is unverified, so the label may be wrong.
materiality: None. The class includes coaches and buses (and heavy lorries), so 'a lorry or bus' describes it correctly, and the numbers are unaffected. Only the project's internal harmonisation note is out of date.
suggested_fix: None needed on the site. Optionally update the note in harmonise.py and ml_common_features.csv to cite the Freginals coach record as evidence that buses are in the class.

title: 'No model has passed every kind of test' is guaranteed by a column that is a population criterion, not a model test
disclosure_where: The Table 1 title, right under the heading ('from the records closest to the fitting data to the comparison of the fitting crashes with those of Spain'). The Table 1 notes at validation.txt:76 define the last column as a Jensen-Shannon limit on variable distributions. The section 'Catalonia's serious crashes differ from Spain's' (validation.txt:53) gives the differences.
factual_core: In validation Table 1, every model shows 'no' in the last column ('Crashes resemble Spain's'). That column is a JSD <= 0.02 comparison of fitting populations, not a ranking test, and no model failed a ranking test it was given. The attacker says the heading 'No model has passed every kind of test' is therefore guaranteed by construction and suggests failures that did not occur.
materiality: None. The heading is literally true, and it matches the page summary ('national use of the models is not established'). The last column is a declared stage of the outward path toward national use, and its 'no' is robust: 0.070 and 0.233 against a 0.02 limit.
suggested_fix: None needed. Optionally add to the heading '(the last column compares populations, not rankings)'.

title: 'Nearly as well as a model fitted there' holds only against a reference restricted to the 11 shared variables
disclosure_where: validation.txt:38 ('the same method restricted to the eleven variables both sources record in the same way'). validation.txt:39 ('against 0.72 for a model of the same kind fitted on DGT's records outside Catalonia'). Figure 2 caption and the Table 2 header ('beside a model of the same kind fitted and cross-validated in the test population'). The summary at validation.txt:9 says 'a model fitted there', and the body qualifies it straight away.
factual_core: The published in-domain reference (0.72) uses only the 11 harmonised variables. A DGT-native model with richer fields (20-code crash type, 4-level zone, road type, owner, 24 hours, vehicles to 6, optionally province) ranks the same 67,971 crashes at about 0.74. So the transferred model (0.71) is about 0.03 below a richer benchmark, not 0.01.
materiality: Against the richer benchmark the gap is -0.028 to -0.035 instead of -0.011. That is still within the study's own 0.05 'ranking held' tolerance, so 'nearly as well' survives. The richer model also leans on fields the study's audit flags: province as a proxy for recording regime, and road type with its 2021 recode.
suggested_fix: None needed. Optionally add one sentence: 'A DGT model using more of DGT's own fields reaches 0.74.'

title: The national ratio partly reflects the mix of networks: within the regional networks it is about 2.5–2.7 in most years
disclosure_where: Not discussed on the page. Methodology §5.1 calls these 'recorded rates by class, not the effect of the class of road'.
factual_core: Most motorway kilometres are on the State network and most conventional-road kilometres on regional and provincial networks. The issue says that inside the regional networks the conventional-to-motorway ratio is about 2.5-2.7 in most years, below the national 3-4.
materiality: No published number or sentence changes. The page explicitly compares classes across all measured networks. Within each network conventional roads still have about 2.6-4.4 times the motorway death rate, and the national ratio (3.04-3.84) lies between the State and regional ratios, so the network mix does not inflate it.
suggested_fix: None required. Optionally add one clause saying that the comparison pools State and regional networks.

title: One dispersion for all months: December's interval is too wide and March and April's too narrow; 'the other months include the average month' fails for December under year-level methods
disclosure_where: The model is named as quasi-Poisson in methodology section 6, and data.html#seasons-months says 'The intervals allow for monthly counts that vary more than chance alone would produce'. That a single dispersion is shared by all months is implicit, not stated.
factual_core: The quasi-Poisson model uses one Pearson dispersion for all 12 months. The attacker says month-specific residual variances differ about sixfold, that the published intervals are therefore miscalibrated month by month, and that methods with month-specific variance put December above 1.
materiality: None demonstrated. The published intervals are valid under a common dispersion, and the data give no evidence against it (p about 0.7). December's interval excluding 1 under t(8) or the bootstrap is the kind of disagreement between two valid methods that occurs by chance in most samples. 'The intervals of the other months include the average month' is true of the published intervals. The March and April conclusions (below 1) hold under every method.
suggested_fix: None required. Optionally, add to the methodology a homogeneity check of the month-specific dispersions (Bartlett p=0.74).

title: Calendar length makes up 44% of February's raw deficit (log scale) and a little of the summer excess; the lead quotes only the unadjusted figures

Also docs/methodology.md:384-386: 'so February's raw effect is partly its 28 days; fuel scales with the days too, so the per-fuel effects are not affected'.

title: '3.4 times' does not equal the printed rates' quotient (15.9 / 4.6 = 3.46, about 3.5)
disclosure_where: No rounding note on the pages; none is needed.
factual_core: The drivers page prints the rates as 15.9 and 4.6 per 1,000 and the ratio as 3.4. The quotient of the printed rates is 3.46, which would round to 3.5, while the ratio of the unrounded rates is 3.431.
materiality: None. 3.4 is the correctly rounded ratio of the counts. 3.46 is a different quantity, the quotient of two rounded figures, and the 45–64 rate rounding down from 4.645 to 4.6 pushes it past 3.45. Printing 3.5 would be the error.
suggested_fix: None needed. Optionally, give the rates as 15.94 and 4.64 where the ratio is quoted.

title: 'Most of all on urban streets' is a relative-scale statement; urban speed crashes are not the deadliest in absolute terms
disclosure_where: Home page: the sentence itself gives the scale, '2.0 times as many deaths per crash as other crashes on the same kind of road, from 1.2 times on dual carriageways to 5.9 times on urban streets'. Speed page: Table 1 prints 4.32, 5.27 and 6.89 deaths per 100 speed crashes. The text below it says the ratio 'was largest on urban streets, where an ordinary injury crash rarely kills (0.73 ... against 4.32)'. The lede says speed crashes are concentrated on other interurban roads, 'where most of their deaths occur'.
factual_core: On the absolute scale, urban speed crashes (4.32 deaths per 100) are less deadly than motorway (5.27) and other interurban (6.89) speed crashes. The urban excess per 100 crashes (3.59) is the highest point estimate but is not clearly separated from other interurban roads (2.96). About 61% of excess deaths are on other interurban roads.
materiality: None. The published statement is on the ratio scale and says so in the same sentence. It is true on that scale with a wide statistical margin, and urban streets also rank first on the absolute-excess point estimate. The site never claims that urban speed crashes are the deadliest, or that most excess deaths are urban.
suggested_fix: None required. If desired: 'deadlier than other crashes on the same kind of road, most of all on urban streets'.

title: The national wet-road odds ratio is pulled down by an outcome-dependent recording pattern in the Catalan provinces' records
disclosure_where: Same as the previous issue. data.html Table 17 prints the full-model wet 0.62 to 0.72 without Catalonia (D2 cites only the CSV link). validation.html says Catalan crashes with a death or serious injury differ on weather and road surface. No page names the severity-dependent surface coding, and severity.html quotes 0.56 unqualified.
factual_core: This is the same artefact as the previous issue: in the Catalan provinces' records, crashes with a death or serious injury (from the Servei Catala de Transit) rarely record a wet surface, while slight crashes record it normally. D2 further claims that without the Catalan records the national wet-surface odds ratio would be about 0.65-0.72 rather than 0.56, a 15-25% weaker effect.
materiality: The headline 0.56 becomes about 0.61 without the artefact (+9% on the odds-ratio scale), not 0.65-0.72. The full-model 0.62 becomes 0.72 (+16%), and that shift is already disclosed on data.html. D2's 'almost never recorded' overstates it: the wet surface appears in 2.3-2.8% of severe Catalan crashes against about 9.7% of slight ones. The direction and every 'below 1' claim hold.
suggested_fix: As for the primary issue: name the Catalan severity-dependent surface coding on severity.html and quote the wet-surface odds ratio without Catalonia, 0.61 (0.54-0.68), or with Catalan surface as its own level, 0.60 (0.53-0.67).

title: Driver-age per-km ratios are printed with a sampling interval only; the averaged-profile interval is narrower than either survey's own and excludes both at 30–44 and 65+

Not stated anywhere: that the two surveys disagree beyond chance at 30-44 and 65+, or that averaging narrows the interval.

title: Interurban deaths per national fuel in 2023: 'outside its range' depends on a symmetric count-scale interval
disclosure_where: The issue says the point is not disclosed, but docs/methodology.md section 5 says 'just outside its range of ±12 %' and data.html gives 13% against ±12%. long-run.html says only 'outside its range'.

title: Policy page still quotes model-based intervals that its own placebos show are about 2.5 times too narrow
disclosure_where: In the policy.html lead, directly next to the quoted average: 'The model's intervals are too narrow: at 6 of the 14 other Julys...'. In the placebo paragraph on the same page: 'An interval set by the spread of the placebo steps puts July 2006 at -21% to +3%, which includes no change'. Not repeated in the heading or in the section 1 sentence that quotes the step interval.

Scaling the step's SE by the placebo ratio 2.46 gives about -21% to +10%, which includes zero, so the heading's 'immediate fall of about 7%' is not established. Two further sub-claims: the calibration uses overlapping placebo windows, and it applies an SD of exp(b)-1 values on the log scale.

title: The pooled speed ratio's interval is said to allow for road-type differences, but understates them several-fold
disclosure_where: speed.html calls 2.00 a weighted summary that 'describes no single kind of road' and is 'weighted towards other interurban roads', next to the interval. The data.html technical notes say 'most of the extra variation the summary's interval allows for is the difference between road types' and give LR 446 on 3 df. The interval's estimand (fixed weighting) is not stated.
factual_core: The page says the 2.00 interval (1.69-2.36) 'is widened to allow for how much the ratios differ', and the Figure 1 caption says it allows 'also for the differences between road types'. In fact it is a common-ratio quasi-Poisson interval: dispersion 13.5 averaged over 52 df, z quantile. An interval that truly allows for between-type variation (random effects) is about 4 times wider in log width, while a fixed-effect interval is narrower, so it matches neither estimand.
materiality: No number changes. The published interval is wider than any fixed-set interval and narrower than random-effects intervals; for the weighted summary the page names, it is conservative. The sentence about the widening and the caption parenthetical overstate what the interval accounts for. As the attacker concedes, every road-type ratio still excludes 1 under the published method, and 2.00 (quasi-Poisson), 2.10 (fixed effect) and 2.22 (random effects) are all 'about 2'.
suggested_fix: Describe the interval by its scope rather than as an allowance for the road-type differences, e.g. 'the interval applies to this weighted summary; it is wider than year-to-year variation alone would make it because one ratio is fitted to unequal road types, and it is not a range for a typical road type'. Amend the Figure 1 caption parenthetical the same way.

title: The home page's heavy-vehicle '2.0 times (1.7–2.2), other circumstances held equal' applies to one reference crash

The Mantel-Haenszel average of 2.24 and the model-standardised 1.97 (1.79–2.16) both support 'about twice'. The variation by crash type confirms heterogeneity, which the published model (heavy x zone only) does not capture. The home-page number does not change.
