title: 'Admissions per tonne of fuel beyond ordinary variation' rests on the 2013–2019 baseline window
Barcelona: speed ranked first among 17 causes on 7 of 38 crashes is not established; the 18.4% is a winner's-curse estimate
disclosure_where: As for F13: barcelona.html gives n = 38 and the per-group interval next to the claim, and data.html Table 23 lists every cause without intervals. Neither mentions selection or how uncertain the ranking is.
factual_core: Speed's first place among the 17–18 causes with at least 30 crashes rests on 7 of 38 crashes. It cannot be told apart from the next causes: Fisher p = 0.11 against the runner-up, Holm-adjusted 0.06–0.11 against the next four. A beta-binomial empirical-Bayes fit shrinks speed to about 6.9%, with P(top) about 0.52, so the 18.4% is inflated by selection (winner's curse).
materiality: The wording change is the same as for F13. The claim that 'the size of the excess (18.4%) is overstated' depends on the model: - The shrinkage to about 7% assumes speed is exchangeable with causes such as careless reversing or lane changes. That prior is worth about 117–135 crashes, centred on 3.7%. - The cause groups overlap (a crash can carry several causes), so they are not independent. - Under flat priors speed is the top cause with probability 0.94. 18.4% is the correct observed share, and the per-group interval is correct as labelled. Speed above the average holds under every analysis.
suggested_fix: As for F13: qualify 'most often' or name the runner-up and say the two cannot be told apart. Optionally add that the largest of 17 small-group shares tends to overstate its group's rate.

title: 'Lleida ... in every year' and 'the lowest share of any lighting condition' are point-estimate rankings, several within chance
disclosure_where: Lleida: no uncertainty is given for the yearly ranks. Lighting: the same paragraph links to Table 18 of the technical notes on data.html, which gives the intervals (lit night 8.8-11.0%, daylight clear 10.6-11.5%, overlapping). Nothing next to the claim says the ranking is close.
factual_core: Lleida's yearly per-resident lead is within chance in 2010, 2018, 2020 and 2022 (two-sided p 0.89, 0.21, 0.55, 0.18). The 'lowest share of any lighting condition' for adequately lit night (9.8%) is not clearly below daylight clear (11.0%, p = 0.067).
materiality: No number changes, and both statements are true point-estimate rankings. The 14/14 pattern and the pooled ranking are robust. 'Lowest' for lit night rests on a 1.2-point gap, p = 0.067. These are wording refinements only.
suggested_fix: 'highest in every year, narrowly in 2010', and 'the highest, and with daylight among the lowest, shares of any lighting condition'.

title: The break rule's 25%/20% threshold decides which runs the headline compares, and the threshold is not calibrated to noise
disclosure_where: factors.html gives the 11% rise in interurban alcohol in 2016 and the 'by 2017' level for manoeuvres. The technical notes call the threshold 'a convention ... so that another threshold can be applied'. methodology.md says 'a rule, not a test with a known error rate'.
factual_core: The fixed 1.25 ratio equals about 5-20 binomial SDs of a one-year log ratio for the large series and 1-2 for drugs. At 1.20, interurban manoeuvres splits (2014-2016 +26%, 2017-2023 -3%). At 1.15, interurban alcohol splits (2014-2018 +19%, 2019-2023 +9%) and so does urban speed (2014-2017 -10%, 2018-2023 -2%). The rule entered in 7897aeb together with the analysis.
materiality: At 1.20 only the interurban-manoeuvres row of Table 1 changes, which duplicates the knife-edge issue. The 1.15 splits change no published sentence. The attacker concedes the alcohol and speed headlines survive at 1.20, and their overdispersed within-run trends exclude zero. The noise-calibration criticism does not apply: year-to-year scatter is 2-140 times binomial, so a rule scaled to binomial SDs would break almost every series. For drugs, a rule that is too sensitive only withholds interpretation, which is the conservative direction.
suggested_fix: Publish the threshold sweep, as for the duplicate, and flag the 2017 jump in illegal manoeuvres as a possible recording step. A dispersion-scaled test is not needed.

title: February's 'interval below 1' per tonne of fuel does not survive a 12-month multiplicity adjustment
disclosure_where: No statement anywhere (pages, methodology, site source) that the twelve month intervals are unadjusted for multiplicity.
factual_core: Per tonne of fuel, February's effect of 0.924 (0.866-0.986) has p=0.017 for its own interval but a Holm-adjusted p of 0.104 over 12 months (BH 0.030). The other six classified months survive Holm.
materiality: Under Holm the section heading would read 'March to May' rather than 'February to May'. Under BH, or the published per-comparison intervals, nothing changes. Printed estimates are unaffected.
suggested_fix: Note that the twelve intervals are per month and unadjusted, or word the heading 'March to May below it (February's interval, the closest to 1, below it only when months are taken one at a time)'.

title: Speed road-type intervals use 1.96 with dispersions estimated on 7 df; with the study's own t-convention the dual-carriageway ratio includes 1
disclosure_where: Same as F9-speed.dual-ci-normal-vs-t. The quantile and the 7 df are stated nowhere; only the 1.02 lower bound in Table 1 hints that the result is borderline.
factual_core: The pooled road-type intervals widen Poisson errors by a Pearson dispersion estimated on 7 residual df but use the normal quantile, while the trends analyses use Student t for the same situation. With t(7) the dual-carriageway interval is 0.98-1.52 (p 0.069), so 'More deaths per crash on every road type' is not supported at 95% for dual carriageways.
materiality: Table 1's dual entry would become 1.22 (0.98-1.52). The heading and the figure text 'Every interval lies above one' would no longer hold for one of four road types. Other types, point estimates and the 2.00 summary are unchanged.
suggested_fix: As for F9-speed.dual-ci-normal-vs-t: use t(df) for the road-type intervals and soften the heading for dual carriageways (e.g. 'on three of four road types; on dual carriageways 1.22, not clearly above 1').

title: The single 'beyond' among 13 comparisons does not survive multiplicity correction, the base year, or the scatter-window choice
'No duplicated rows' holds only for exact copies; a handful of records look like the same crash entered twice
disclosure_where: DATA_QUALITY_MICRODATA.md:233-248 reports 0 full duplicates and keeps the 14 time-only rows, with a reason. data.html (Catalonia notes) says 'it has no duplicated rows'. Pairs that share the time but differ in coded fields are not mentioned.
factual_core: Besides the 14 rows identical in everything but the time, a handful of record pairs on real roads share the date, municipality, road, kilometre point and every casualty and unit count. They differ in coded fields, and most share the same minute. One is a fatal pair 2 minutes apart. 'No duplicated rows' therefore holds only for exact copies.
materiality: About 9 rows (0.04%) and 1 fatal crash; no published share moves.
suggested_fix: Same as D7: 'no row is an exact copy; about fifty records repeat another crash's date, time, place and casualty counts and are probably double records; they are kept'.

title: The person model's gain over its table on the pre-declared test depends on the outcome-recording crash-type code
disclosure_where: The gain over the table appears only in generated documents: MODEL_DECISIONS.md ('adds signal'), docs/models/barcelona_person_severity.md ('The model adds signal over the table') and ML_MODEL_REVIEW.md:56 ('It ranks people better than the table'). None of them mentions the code. barcelona.html discloses the code only for the crash model, as the attacker says. But validation.html does disclose it for the person model, qualitatively, next to the district score, so 'disclosed: no' is too strong.
factual_core: On the pre-declared months 10-12 test, the person model's gain over the role x vehicle table is +0.063 (+0.020 to +0.106). With Encalç merged into Abast it falls to about +0.02, with an interval that includes 0, so it fails the pre-declared 'adds signal' rule. accident_type is a top permutation-importance feature and is labelled 'safe'.
materiality: Nothing on the site states the person model's gain over the table. Under the pre-declared rules the documented decision changes from 'KEEP but ranking-only' to 'REPLACE with descriptive table'. The review's 'ranks people better than the table' loses support. Its status (research only, no probabilities) is unchanged.
suggested_fix: Refit the person model with Encalç merged, or relabel accident_type as outcome-dependent for Barcelona. Then restate the gain (+0.024, -0.020 to +0.064, no measurable gain) in MODEL_DECISIONS.md, the model card and ML_MODEL_REVIEW.md.

title: "Ranked crashes no better than the shares by crash type" reads a 58-case non-significant test as evidence of no gain
disclosure_where: The interval is in docs/models/barcelona_crash_severity.md:118, docs/MODEL_DECISIONS.md:34,97 and ml_rule_comparison.csv (linked at the foot of data.html). It is not on barcelona.html, severity-models.html or validation.html. data.html gives the design next to the claim, but not the size or interval.
factual_core: Same claim and same evidence as F13-barcelona.crash-model-no-better-underpowered. The attacker says 'ranked crashes no better' reads a non-significant 58-case test (gain +0.003, -0.039 to +0.051) as evidence of no gain. It adds that with all 252 positives the model shows a small gain that meets the adds-signal rule under leave-one-district-out.
materiality: As for the F13 issue: the wording changes from 'no better' to 'not shown to rank better (gain +0.003, 95% interval -0.04 to +0.05, 58 serious crashes)'. The full-year gain is small and positive, about +0.01 to +0.02 within folds, and passes the rule only with pooled scoring. The decision to show the table stands.
suggested_fix: Say 'was not shown to rank better than the shares by crash type (gain +0.003, 95% interval -0.04 to +0.05, 58 serious crashes)' wherever the claim appears.

title: Driver risk comparison states per-km age and sex ratios as findings, without the sensitivity ranges or the 75+ condition the study says they need
'Within ordinary variation' for deaths could not have detected changes smaller than about 15%
disclosure_where: Table 1 and Figure 1 on trends.html, directly under the heading 'Deaths changed within ordinary variation under every denominator', print every interval: count -8.3% to +12.9%, per tonne -6.7% to +14.9%, per vehicle -13.2% to +19.1%. The summary sentence prints none. No power or detectable-change statement appears anywhere; the detectable changes of the withdrawn forecast were withdrawn with it. data.html notes that the deaths dispersion interval (0.6–8.7) includes 1. The page limitation says denominators are treated as exact.
factual_core: Under the published construction (dispersion 1.45, 1.00 or 2.35; Student's t with 5 df), a change in deaths is flagged 80% of the time only beyond about +15.3%/-13.3% (count, per resident, per tonne), +17.1%/-14.6% (drivers per licence holder) and +24.1%/-19.4% (occupants per vehicle). 'Within ordinary variation' is therefore a non-rejection that is compatible with rises of up to about 13–19%.
materiality: No number changes and the verdict stands. The only effect is on wording: the summary's 'under every denominator the change lies within the variation of an ordinary year' could add that changes of up to about +13% to +19% are not ruled out. The intervals beside the claim already carry this information.
suggested_fix: In the summary, write 'under every denominator the change is not distinguishable from an ordinary year's variation (the intervals run up to about +9% to +19%)'.

title: The crude 3.4 ratio partly reflects that most drivers aged 75 and over are men; adjusted for sex and zone it is about 2.9
disclosure_where: As for D2: no page or document relates the sex or zone mix to the age contrast. The drivers page gives only the sex gap within age bands.
factual_core: Same core as D2: the crude 3.4 partly reflects the 84.6% (75+) against 64.0% (45–64) male share. In 2014–2021 it also partly reflects a higher interurban share at 75+. Adjusted for sex and zone, the 2024 ratio is about 2.9, and pooled 2014–2024 it falls from 3.58 to about 2.78.
materiality: As for D2: about 3.0 (sex) or 2.93 (sex and zone) against the published 3.43 for 2024. The conclusion is unchanged, since the adjusted lower bound is 2.2. Zone matters for earlier and pooled years, not for the published 2024 figure. Note that the attacker's 'intervals do not overlap' (crude against adjusted from the same data) is not a valid test of difference, and adjusting for zone may remove part of what describes older drivers (where they drive). The defensible core is the sex part, about 13%.
suggested_fix: Same as D2: give the sex-adjusted or within-sex ratio beside the crude 3.4.
